Senmiao Technology filed its 10-Q with the SEC disclosing that starting in 2026 the company began evaluating expansion into AI infrastructure, appointed David Nichols as strategic advisor for power infrastructure and capital formation, and in July 2026 formed Nebula Matrix AI LLC (90% owned) with Constant Energy Construction Corp. to develop AI data centers in the U.S.

projects.name: Andover HPC Data Center
projects.note: National Land Developers registered Andover HPC Development in December 2025 at 248 Stickles Pond Road, a 97-acre former airport site. Andover Township first allowed data centers in a redevelopment zone along Route 206 (September 2025) and raised the height limit to 65 feet (April 2026), but after a chaotic May 2026 meeting with 300 residents, the township passed Ordinance 2026-13 banning data centers township-wide. No formal site plan was ever filed. National Land Developers sued in Sussex County Superior Court on July 10, 2026, challenging the ban.

events.summary: In September 2021 the Township Committee adopted Resolution 2021-91, designating approximately 812 acres along the Route 206 corridor (43 tax lots, including the Stickles Pond Road parcel) as a Non-Condemnation Area in Need of Redevelopment.
In 2024 the 97-acre property at 248 Stickles Pond Road received approval for a 660,000-square-foot warehouse development with little public opposition.
In August 2025 township officials first publicly discussed a potential data center at a committee meeting.
Township passes ordinance allowing data centers in Route 206 redevelopment zone.
Approximately 33 days after the September 2025 ordinance permitting data centers, the property owner satisfied a $1.28 million mortgage on the Stickles Pond Road parcel.
Andover HPC Development LLC registered at 248 Stickles Pond Road address.
Township committee votes to raise height limit to 65 feet in redevelopment zone.

Attorney Anand Dash, representing community group Andover Responsible Development (a fiscally sponsored member of the NJ Highlands Coalition), filed a legal notice challenging Ordinances 2025-15 and 2026-08 as violations of state Municipal Land Use Law, threatening suit if they were not rescinded by May 7.
Chaotic meeting with ~300 residents opposing data center; police confrontation.

At the same contentious meeting, the Township Committee voted 4-1 to introduce an ordinance creating additional data center standards including closed-loop water cooling, noise controls, and electric substation requirements; five days later they reversed course and introduced a ban instead.

NJTODAY reported that the township attorney confirmed preliminary PILOT financial discussions had taken place behind closed doors, and identified recently formed entities Bridge AIX LLC and Bridge AI Group LLC linked to the project through Delaware registrations.
Mayor Tom Walsh posted a video statement saying the Township Committee had directed the township attorney to draft an ordinance repealing data centers as a permitted use.
At a special meeting the Township Committee introduced Ordinance 2026-13, a township-wide data center ban that would repeal the two prior ordinances permitting them.
The Andover Township Land Use Board found Ordinance 2026-13 consistent with the township's master plan.
The Township Committee unanimously adopted Ordinance 2026-13, prohibiting data centers as a use in all zones townshipwide.
National Land Developers files lawsuit in Sussex County Superior Court challenging Ordinance 2026-13 banning data centers.
Andover officials said they intend to vigorously defend the ordinance, have no interest in settling, and expect to file a response to the complaint within about 30 days.
The Sussex County Democratic Committee issued a written statement criticizing township officials over the ordinance's vulnerability to the developer's lawsuit.

Insider NJ reported Mayor Walsh stated the township has funding in place to defend the ordinance; Sussex County Republican chair Joseph LaBarbera denied Democratic allegations that the GOP was lobbying for data centers, calling the claim a deliberate lie.

projects.name: Pennhurst Data Center Campus
projects.note: Penn Hurst Holdings proposed a 1.9 million-square-foot data center campus on 123 acres of the historic Pennhurst State School and Hospital site. The East Vincent Township Board of Supervisors voted unanimously to deny the conditional use application on May 21, 2026. Penn Hurst Holdings appealed to Chester County Court of Common Pleas on June 26, arguing irreconcilable contradictions in the township's zoning code.

events.summary: East Vincent Board of Supervisors unanimously denies conditional use application for 1.9M sq ft data center.
Township issues written denial decision.
Penn Hurst Holdings files appeal to Chester County Court of Common Pleas.

projects.name: Karis Critical Plum Farms Data Center
projects.note: Karis Critical acquired 180 acres known as Plum Farms at the northwest corner of Route 59 and Higgins Road for $45 million and sought rezoning for a data center. The village planning commission gave a negative recommendation in early June 2026. After weeks of community backlash, Karis notified the village on July 1 that it would withdraw the rezoning request. Governor Pritzker had also suspended state data center incentives. Karis has not indicated whether it will refile.

events.summary: Village planning commission votes against rezoning recommendation.
Karis Critical withdraws rezoning request after community opposition.

projects.name: Site Layer 4 Data Center Campus
projects.note: Site Layer 4, a New York-based firm, has applied to rezone 5,344 acres of ranchland on the Lazy V Six Ranch northeast of Wheatland for a $26 billion data center campus with co-located utility-scale energy generation. The project promises 300 jobs and substantial tax revenue but neighbors are concerned about water, wildlife, and viewshed impacts. More than 400 public comments were received. Planning and Zoning Commission hearing rescheduled to August 26, 2026, with County Commissioners hearing on September 2.

events.summary: Rezoning application revealed for 5,344-acre data center campus on Lazy V Six Ranch.
Planning and Zoning Commission public hearing at Agriplex, Wheatland.
Platte County Commissioners public hearing at Agriplex, Wheatland.

projects.name: Project Bluestem
projects.note: Cloverleaf Infrastructure proposes Project Bluestem, a 600 MW hyperscale data center on approximately 1,000 acres of former Tailgate Ranch land south of Tonganoxie. The Leavenworth County Commission passed a 90-day moratorium on data center applications in May 2026, which expired in August. On August 5, commissioners voted 3-2 against extending the moratorium. On August 13, officials reversed course and directed planning and zoning to delay regulation recommendations until after a joint work session before the September meeting. No formal application has been submitted.

events.summary: Leavenworth County residents pack public forum on proposed data center.

Coverage identified Cloverleaf Infrastructure as the developer of Project Bluestem, a conceptual 1,000-acre data center near Tonganoxie that could require up to 1.2 gigawatts of power and would receive a 100% sales and use tax abatement for 20 years, with no formal applications yet submitted.

The opposition group Citizens Against Bluestem held its inaugural meeting at the Tonganoxie VFW Post Home, drawing roughly 150 attendees; speakers included County Commissioner Mike Stieben and a Sierra Club representative.
Leavenworth County Commission passes 90-day moratorium on data center applications.
The Tongie Data Center Watch Dog Group planned to present a petition to the Tonganoxie City Council at 7 p.m. on Monday, May 19, seeking an 18-month moratorium on data center development.
Project Bluestem representatives held an open house at 304 Venue in Tonganoxie to address resident concerns about the proposed data center.
Commission votes 3-2 against extending moratorium; moratorium expires.
Officials reverse course, direct P&Z to delay recommendations until joint work session in September.
About 100 protesters organized by the Tongie Data Center WatchDog Group packed the Leavenworth County planning meeting, where the planning commission voted 8-1 to revisit data center regulations.

projects.name: Muncy Township Data Center
projects.note: DANKO Holdings II / Fishlips LLC filed a zoning permit application on April 15, 2026, and a conditional use application on April 28, for three data center buildings along John Brady Drive near Yetter Road, about two miles east of the closed Lycoming Mall. The township failed to hold the required hearing within 60 days, and the developer published a legal notice in July claiming 'deemed approval' under the state Municipalities Planning Code. Supervisors imposed a nine-month moratorium on data center submissions in June 2026. The legal status of the deemed-approval claim is unresolved.

events.summary: Zoning permit application filed by DANKO Holdings II / Fishlips LLC.
Conditional use application filed for three data center buildings.
Township supervisors impose nine-month moratorium on data center submissions.
Developer publishes legal notice claiming deemed approval due to township's failure to hold hearing within 60 days.

projects.name: Urbana Technology Hub
projects.note: Thor Equities assembled approximately 230 acres near Ohio 55 and US 68 for a 460,000 sq ft, $1B+ data center campus called the Urbana Technology Hub. A site plan application was submitted February 13 but deemed incomplete by city staff. The BZA unanimously denied Thor's appeal. The city council then adopted new zoning codes removing data centers as a permitted use in the M-1 manufacturing district. Thor Equities filed a federal lawsuit in the US District Court for the Southern District of Ohio. A charter amendment petition and mayor recall effort are also underway.

events.summary: Urbana City Council approved a zoning code modification permitting data centers in the M-1 Light Manufacturing District and annexed Thor Equities' property.
Urbana Owner I LLC (linked to Thor Equities) purchased a 47.6-acre parcel near the proposed site for $2,143,665.
In November 2025, city council approved a Community Reinvestment Area (CRA2) tax abatement agreement for the data center site after three readings.
Highland55 Investments LLC purchased 85.6 acres southwest of Urbana for $3,210,712.50, the second major land assembly for the campus.
City Director of Administration Spencer Mitchell publicly confirmed for the first time that a property owner had approached the city about developing a data center.
Council members discussed data center concerns at a regular meeting and directed Law Director Feinstein to prepare moratorium legislation for the February 17 meeting.
Site plan application submitted by Choice One Engineering on behalf of Thor Equities; deemed incomplete by city staff.
City council voted 5-2 to remove a proposed 12-month data center moratorium from the agenda; approximately 50 residents attended the meeting.
Data center plans revealed at city meeting.
Thor Equities issued a public statement on the proposed data center, describing it as a $1 billion private investment and pledging water conservation, stable electric rates, and community investment.
Urbana City Council passed a 12-month moratorium on new data centers by a 6-1 vote, with Audra Bean the sole dissenter; about 40 residents spoke afterward mostly in support.

Ideastream reported the moratorium left the $1 billion proposal in limbo and identified CyrusOne as a project partner alongside Thor Equities; an online petition opposing the project had gathered over 4,000 signatures within two weeks.
Thor Equities formally appeals city's determination that application was incomplete.
BZA unanimously denies Thor's appeal, upholding city determination that site plan application was incomplete.
Thor Equities launched a project information website, urbanaohiodatacenter.com, with a project overview, economic-benefit claims, and a contact form.

Thor Equities publicized economic-impact figures for the project: over $1 billion investment, more than $5.8 million in annual local tax revenue, over 1,000 construction jobs, and 30 to 80 permanent positions.
City council adopts new zoning codes removing data centers as permitted use in M-1 district.
Thor Equities purchased approximately 97 acres from Organ Farms LLC for about $3.4 million, adding a southern access point from U.S. Highway 68 to the proposed campus.
A public hearing was held on the proposed ordinance to reverse the 2025 zoning amendment and remove data centers as a permitted use in the M-1 district.
City council unanimously passed Ordinance 4635-26, restoring the pre-2025 zoning code and completing the removal of data centers as a permitted M-1 use; residents applauded the vote.
Thor Equities files federal lawsuit against City of Urbana in US District Court, Southern District of Ohio.

In July 2026, Thor Equities launched a direct mail, television, and digital advertising campaign aimed at Urbana residents, describing it as an educational effort to counter misinformation about the project.

Two Urbana residents launched petitions: Nicole Nawman began a charter-amendment petition to bar hyperscale data centers, and James Cropper began a petition to recall Mayor Bill Bean over alleged lack of transparency.
City Law Director Mark Feinstein submitted his resignation to Mayor Bean, effective August 7, 2026, citing a new legal opportunity and family priorities; the city began recruiting a replacement.
Nicole Nawman turned in the charter-amendment petition packet to the Champaign County Board of Elections, saying signatures well surpassed the required minimum.
The Champaign County Board of Elections reported the mayoral recall petitions collected enough valid signatures for the recall question to appear on the November 3 general election ballot.

A Champaign County Common Pleas judge ordered the city to provide a complete transcript of the April 13 BZA hearing and set briefing deadlines through October 2026; the ruling did not decide the merits of the case.

Urbana City Council approved emergency Ordinance No. 4640-26, sending the proposed data-center-ban charter amendment to the November 3, 2026 ballot, suspending rules to meet the August 5 filing deadline.

Three candidates filed petitions by the August 5 deadline to replace Mayor Bean if he is recalled; Eugene Fields Jr. and Nicole Nawman met the 169-signature threshold while Taylor Armstrong fell four signatures short.

The Champaign County Board of Elections forwarded the charter-amendment petition to the Ohio Secretary of State after finding a typographical error referencing Article VII instead of Article VIII, leaving its ballot status uncertain.

projects.name: Colossus 2
projects.note: Chip types: B200,B300. Epoch AI estimates ~946 MW.

events.summary: xAI announced it had begun installing computing infrastructure at its expanded Southwest Memphis data center on Tulane Road, called Colossus 2, saying 110,000 Nvidia GB200 GPUs were being installed.
Earthjustice and the Southern Environmental Law Center announced they had sent xAI a 60-day Clean Air Act notice of intent to sue over unpermitted gas turbines in Southaven powering Colossus 2.

A Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality public hearing in Southaven on xAI's permit for 41 permanent gas turbines drew hundreds of attendees and, per the report, unanimous opposition from residents citing noise and air-pollution concerns.

The Mississippi Environmental Quality Permit Board unanimously granted xAI affiliate MZX Tech an air permit to install 41 methane gas-fired turbines at its Southaven facility, over community opposition.

The Mississippi State Conference of the NAACP and the national NAACP, represented by SELC and Earthjustice, filed suit against xAI and its subsidiary MZX Tech in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Mississippi, alleging illegal operation of unpermitted gas turbines under the Clean Air Act.

The NAACP filed a request for a preliminary injunction asking the court to immediately halt xAI's unpermitted air pollution from what it called an illegal power plant, then powering Colossus 2 with 33 unpermitted gas turbines.

The U.S. Department of Justice moved to intervene in the NAACP lawsuit and asked the court to dismiss it, arguing that shutting off power to the Colossus 2 data center would harm national security because xAI's Grok supports Department of Defense military operations.

Records obtained via public-records request (Trinity Consultants emails to Mississippi regulators) revealed xAI had operated 59 unpermitted gas turbines for Colossus 2, roughly double the 27 the company had publicly acknowledged in January, with at least 57 sited in Southaven, Mississippi.

The Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality issued an agreed order setting a retirement schedule for xAI's 69 temporary trailer-mounted turbines at the Southaven site, requiring decommissioning to begin August 18, 2026, with most units retired by April 2027 and the most recently added by July 14, 2027, after supply-chain delays to the 41 permanent turbines.

projects.name: Microsoft Fairwater Atlanta
projects.note: Part of Microsoft AI WAN. Chip types: B200. Epoch AI estimates ~636 MW.

events.summary: Fayetteville City Council voted 5-0 to annex and rezone 412 acres from R-70 residential to Business Park for a data center office park, with 18 rezoning conditions attached; approximately 24 residents spoke in opposition, some in tears.

QTS purchased 615 acres in Fayetteville for $153.8 million (approximately $250,000 per acre) from the Fayette County Development Authority, brokered by CBRE, for what it called the world's largest multi-tenant data center campus.

QTS publicly announced Project Excalibur: a planned 6.6 million sq ft campus of 16 data center buildings plus 400,000 sq ft of office space on the 615-acre Fayetteville site, with construction to start in 2023 and full build-out by 2032, investing over $1 billion.

Fayetteville Planning and Zoning Commission approved the conceptual site plan and schematic building elevations for the Excalibur Data Center after a 5-6 month Development of Regional Impact review involving GDOT and the Georgia Department of Community Affairs.
Land clearing began at the QTS Project Excalibur site in April 2023, per Epoch AI satellite imagery analysis.

Fayetteville City Council unanimously approved a development agreement between the City and National Acquisition Company, LLC (QTS affiliate) for the 612-acre data center campus at 1435 Highway 54 West.

The Fayette County Development Authority proposed 'Project Rita,' a 96 MW data center campus on 145.5 acres in Tyrone (adjacent to the QTS site), comprising two buildings totaling 490,000 sq ft with a requested Business Technology Park rezoning; the Town Council hearing was scheduled for March 21.

Tyrone Town Council approved the rezoning for the Microsoft data center (Project Rita) on approximately 147 acres on North Highway 74, following Planning Commission and Town Council public hearings on February 22 and March 21 respectively.
The first building on the QTS campus received its certificate of occupancy in May 2025, per the AJC, with a construction completion certificate issued September 25, 2025.

Fayette County Water System sent a letter to QTS revealing that a water meter installed during a system-wide smart-meter upgrade had not been read electronically, resulting in approximately 13 million gallons of unrecorded usage and a retroactive bill of approximately $147,000; the issue was discovered after a neighbor reported low water pressure.
Microsoft's Fairwater 2 data center on the QTS campus began operations in October 2025, spanning more than 1 million sq ft and using closed-loop cooling described as consuming almost zero water.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella announced the Fayetteville facility as part of the world's first AI superfactory, connecting the Atlanta Fairwater 2 site with Fairwater 1 in Wisconsin across a single flat network to train AI models at planet scale.

In January 2026 Fayetteville City Council passed a 90-day moratorium on new data center development applications while working to revise the Unified Development Ordinance; City Manager Ray Gibson stated 'we do not want anymore data centers in our community.'

WBRC reported on community impacts from the QTS/Microsoft campus, with resident Diana Dietz citing heavy truck traffic on residential roads, transmission lines through neighborhoods, and concerns over rising power and water bills; QTS stated it uses water-free cooling and is committed to paying its fair share of power costs.

Crow Holdings Development withdrew its appeal of a denied data center project on Highway 85 North in Fayetteville one day before the scheduled City Council hearing; the city had also enacted UDO changes on March 5 that made data centers no longer permissible.

QTS Fayetteville I DC1-2, LLC began sounding out investors for $5.4 billion in new debt ($4.9 billion secured bond plus $500 million term loan) to finance expansion of the Fayetteville campus leased to Microsoft, under an updated green bond framework with a PUE threshold tightened from 1.5 to 1.4.

projects.name: Anthropic-Amazon New Carlisle
projects.note: Part of Project Rainier. Chip types: Trainium2. Epoch AI estimates ~910 MW.

events.summary: St. Joseph County Redevelopment Commission approved Resolution 2023-16, a development facilitation agreement between the Commission, the Indiana Economic Development Corporation, and Razor5 LLC for pre-development activities on 640 acres in the New Carlisle Economic Development Area.

Local media reported construction activity already underway on the Razor5 site near New Carlisle, including an electrical substation pad on 45 acres near Edison Road and excavation on the northern parcel, before the developer's identity was publicly confirmed.

St. Joseph County Area Plan Commission voted 6-1 to give a favorable recommendation for rezoning over 800 acres at 31000 State Road 2 from agricultural to industrial classification for the Razor5 project, sparking complaints from New Carlisle residents.

St. Joseph County Council voted 8-1 to rezone approximately 640 acres of agricultural land near New Carlisle to industrial use for the Razor5 LLC project, with Council Republican Joe Thomas casting the lone dissenting vote.

Tax abatement proposal documents presented to the St. Joseph County Council revealed the Razor5 project would total $11 billion in investment across 640 acres and a secondary 280-acre parcel, projecting 400 full-time jobs at approximately $30 per hour.

Governor Eric Holcomb announced Amazon Web Services plans to invest $11 billion to build a data center campus near New Carlisle, the largest capital investment in Indiana history, with at least 1,000 jobs over 10 years; state incentives included up to $18.3 million in tax credits, $55 million in Hoosier Business Investment credits, and $7 million for State Road 2 improvements.

St. Joseph County Council committee voted a favorable recommendation on the Amazon data center tax abatement declaratory resolution, advancing it to the full county council for a public hearing scheduled for June 11.

St. Joseph County Council voted 7-2 to approve the Amazon data center incentive package: a 10-year 50% real property tax abatement on 870 acres, an 85% enterprise technology exemption on personal property for 35 years, and a community enhancement agreement valued at approximately $143 million.

Amazon held a ceremonial groundbreaking for Project Rainier at Century Center in South Bend, attended by Governor Holcomb and AWS VP Kevin Miller; construction on the 870-acre site had already been underway for months prior to the ceremony.

In September 2025, the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission unanimously approved the creation of NIPSCO Generation LLC (GenCo), described as America's first data center-only utility subsidiary, to generate and sell electricity exclusively to hyperscale data centers including the Amazon New Carlisle campus.

Amazon announced Project Rainier was operational in New Carlisle with seven data center buildings running approximately 500,000 Trainium2 chips dedicated to training Anthropic's Claude AI models, making it the largest known deployment of non-Nvidia compute in the world.

Amazon announced an additional $15 billion investment in new data center campuses across northern Indiana, bringing total committed investment to approximately $26 billion, with a NIPSCO energy deal projected to save existing ratepayers $1 billion over 15 years.

NIPSCO filed plans to supply up to 3 GW to Amazon data centers in northern Indiana through GenCo, which will build two 1.3-GW gas-fired power plants and a 400-MW battery storage system, with power deliveries beginning January 1, 2027, and ramping to 2.4 GW by end of 2032.

Four Republican members of the St. Joseph County Council sent Amazon a letter asking it to renegotiate its 35-year property tax abatement, citing Microsoft's national policy of forgoing local tax breaks and the region's inherent advantages including one of the nation's richest aquifers.

Amazon granted local media the first look at the New Carlisle data center campus administration building and workforce development programs; the first work-based learning cohort of 58 local graduates had completed training in machine learning and data center operations.

AWS announced its New Carlisle campus investment had reached $13.8 billion with 18 of approximately 30 planned buildings operational, over 1,000 employees hired (approximately 450 from St. Joseph County), and up to 4,000 construction workers on site during peak phases.

projects.name: Meta Prometheus
projects.note: Part of Prometheus. Chip types: B200. Epoch AI estimates ~562 MW.

events.summary: Meta announced a further expansion of its New Albany data center campus, adding buildings that brought total investment in Ohio to more than $1.5 billion and supporting 300 operational jobs and 1,200 peak construction workers.

Power Engineering reported that Will-Power (Williams Companies) had filed with the Ohio Power Siting Board for two behind-the-meter natural gas plants, Socrates North and Socrates South, each 200 MW, at Meta's New Albany International Business Park campus, with a planned in-service date of Q3 2026.

The Ohio Power Siting Board approved the Socrates South Power Generation Project, a 200 MW behind-the-meter natural gas plant in Licking County to be built by Will-Power OH (a Williams Companies subsidiary) to serve exclusively Sidecat, part of Meta Platforms, on its 740-acre New Albany Business Park campus.

Power Engineering reported that construction on the Socrates South 200 MW natural gas plant serving Sidecat (Meta) in New Albany was planned to begin in June 2025 with expected completion in November 2026, detailing the turbine fleet including Solar Turbines Titan 250s, Siemens SGT400s, and Caterpillar reciprocating engines.

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg announced on Threads and Facebook that Meta's first AI supercluster, Prometheus, a 1-gigawatt data center in New Albany, Ohio, will come online in 2026, alongside a larger Hyperion cluster and hundreds of billions of dollars in compute investment.

A Meta engineering blog post described Prometheus as a 1-gigawatt cluster spanning multiple traditional data center buildings plus weatherproof tents and adjacent colocation facilities, and said the buildout was currently underway.

In early November 2025, Turner Construction evacuated over 1,000 workers from the Prometheus data center construction site in New Albany after a terminated contractor returned and threatened a supervisor with a firearm; security confiscated the weapon and law enforcement responded.

Spectrum News 1 reported on Meta's Prometheus in New Albany as potentially the world's first gigawatt-scale data center, noting on-site gas-fired power plants; Mayor Sloan Spalding said the facility would not draw energy off the grid, and residents raised concerns about local power reliability.

Meta announced nuclear energy agreements with Oklo, Vistra and TerraPower for up to 6.6 GW by 2035, stating the projects will deliver power to grids supporting its operations including the Prometheus supercluster in New Albany, Ohio.

WOSU reported that a University of Virginia/Joyce Foundation study found Columbus will become the second-largest data center hub in the Great Lakes region behind Chicago, noting Meta is wrapping up construction on its Prometheus gigawatt-scale data center in New Albany and that Ohio data centers currently consume 5.3% of the state's energy, projected to reach 10.9% within four years.

Corning and Meta announced a multiyear agreement worth up to $6 billion for Corning to supply optical fiber, cable, and connectivity solutions for Meta's U.S. data center buildout, with Corning expanding its Hickory, North Carolina, manufacturing facility where Meta will be the anchor customer.

The American Prospect reported that Meta opened its first Ohio data center in 2017 under the operating name Sidecat LLC after state lawmakers approved $37 million in tax breaks, and that Meta plans to open its one-gigawatt Prometheus AI cluster housed in five or more buildings in 2026.

Energies Media reported that Williams expects to bring each of its Socrates power generation facilities in New Albany online around the end of 2026, with construction anticipated to begin during 2025 and a one-year commissioning period following construction start.

Governor DeWine ordered the Ohio Tax Credit Authority to pause consideration of new data center sales tax exemption requests after the state underestimated the 2025 cost of the exemption by more than $1.4 billion, directing the pause to take effect after the Authority's June 1 meeting while a Joint Data Center Committee studies the issue.

The Ohio Power Siting Board authorized construction of the Socrates the Younger (STY) Power Generation Facility, a 250 MW natural gas plant with 116 MW battery storage on 109 acres in Licking County, New Albany, to serve Sidecat LLC (Meta) behind-the-meter, subject to 36 conditions.

Mark Zuckerberg announced the $1 billion Future Is for Everyone Fund to invest in communities where Meta owns or is building data centers, including New Albany, targeting locally identified priorities such as schools, teachers, first responders, and energy and water infrastructure.

Earthwork and excavation began on the Microsoft data center site in Mount Pleasant, with Walsh Construction (Chicago) leading construction services on the 215-acre campus.

Microsoft announced a $3.3 billion investment in an AI data center campus in Mount Pleasant; President Biden joined Microsoft President Brad Smith at Gateway Technical College for the announcement, which included 2,300 union construction jobs and a 250 MW solar project.
Microsoft paused construction on portions of its Mount Pleasant data center site, stating it was 'refining our data center design'; the first phase remained on track for 2026 completion.

Microsoft paused construction again on a 900-acre expansion area west of the main campus, citing evaluation of 'scope and recent changes in technology'; the company's $3.3 billion commitment and first-phase 2026 timeline remained intact.

Microsoft announced an additional $4 billion investment for a second data center in Mount Pleasant, bringing total Wisconsin investment to over $7 billion; the second facility is expected to be completed by 2028.

Caledonia Plan Commission voted 5-2 to rezone 245 acres from agricultural to light industrial for Microsoft's third data center (Project Nova) near the We Energies Oak Creek Power Plant, after more than 40 residents spoke against it.

Microsoft proposed a $13.3 billion expansion in Mount Pleasant with two new campuses totaling 15 data centers across more than 1,300 acres, potentially generating over $76 million in annual property tax revenue.

Mount Pleasant Village Board unanimously approved site plans for 15 additional Microsoft data centers on two campuses (9 buildings on 791 acres near Durand Avenue, 6 buildings on 530 acres along International Drive), with anticipated power demand of approximately 2 gigawatts when fully developed.
In April 2026, Microsoft brought equipment online and began startup activities at the Fairwater data center, its first facility in Mount Pleasant.

Microsoft announced the Fairwater data center in Mount Pleasant is fully operational, calling it 'the world's most powerful supercomputer'; the 1.2-million-square-foot facility employs approximately 550 full-time workers and was built by nearly 10,000 construction workers over two years.

Three Sturtevant residents filed a class-action lawsuit against Microsoft in U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Wisconsin, alleging significant noise pollution from diesel generators and HVAC systems at the Fairwater data center, seeking to represent over 1,000 households within 1.5 miles.

projects.name: Google Columbus

High Street; council members did not learn the applicant was Google until months later.

In May 2021 Google, operating as Magellan Enterprises LLC, purchased the 480-acre former Hartman Stock Farm property at 5076 S. High Street in Columbus for more than $30 million, according to Franklin County Auditor records.

Google broke ground on its $300 million, 150,000-square-foot Columbus data center at the former Hartman Farm site, ahead of schedule, with an expected completion by end of 2025 and 20 permanent jobs; the company also signed a Good Neighbor Agreement with the Far South Columbus Area Commission to preserve roughly one-third of the 496-acre site as green space.

Google publicly confirmed plans for two new data centers in Columbus (5076 S. High St., ~500 acres, ~$300 million) and Lancaster (104 Whiley Road, ~120 acres, $120 million) as part of its over-$2 billion total Ohio investment since 2019.

Google announced an additional $1.7 billion investment across its three central Ohio data center campuses in Columbus, Lancaster, and New Albany to complete the Columbus and Lancaster facilities and expand New Albany, bringing total Ohio data center investment past $2 billion.

The Google Lockbourne data center at 5076 S. High Street in Columbus became fully operational in 2024, comprising four buildings (Metro Park, Cloud Center, Cloud Ridge, and Cloud Station) on the campus.

Google announced an additional $2.3 billion investment in its three central Ohio data center campuses (Columbus, New Albany, Lancaster) for cloud services and AI infrastructure, bringing total Ohio investment past $4.4 billion since 2019.

In November 2024 the Columbus City Council voted 9-0 to raise water and sewer rates; Google's Far South Side data center consumed 177 million gallons of water in 2024 during its first year of operation.

Google signed a 15-year power purchase agreement with TotalEnergies for the 49-MW Montpelier solar farm in Williams County, Ohio, to supply 1.5 TWh of renewable electricity to its Ohio data center operations.

WOSU reported that data centers are a main driver of rising utility costs in Columbus, with AEP Ohio, Columbia Gas, and Columbus Water all seeking rate increases projected to add $36/month for average customers by 2027; PUCO held public hearings in December 2025.

The Columbus Free Press reported that Google's Far South Side facility used 177 million gallons of water in 2024, documented visible steam emissions near residential areas, and quoted former Far South Side area commissioner Bruce Miller saying hundreds of resident voices were ignored during the approval process.

projects.name: Google New Albany

In December 2018, the Ohio Tax Credit Authority approved a 100%, 15-year sales tax exemption for Google's Montauk Innovations data center project, valued at approximately $43.5 million over the life of the credit and renewable for up to 40 years.
Holder Construction broke ground on November 1, 2019 on Google's $600 million data center on 440 acres in New Albany, part of Google's $13 billion 2019 expansion plan for seven new U.S. data centers.

New Albany's incentive package for Google included 100% property tax abatement for 15 years and a waiver of up to $250,000 in building and permitting fees, with a minimum annual revenue generation requirement of $750,000 beginning in 2021.
Google's New Albany data center was completed and became operational in 2021, according to property records listing the year built as 2021.

On August 20, 2021, Google announced an additional $1 billion investment to expand its New Albany data center campus and disclosed it had acquired 618 more acres (500 in Columbus, approximately 120 in Lancaster) for potential future data centers, bringing total Ohio acreage to over 1,000.

Google launched its Columbus Ohio cloud region (us-east5) on May 24, 2022, its 2nd Midwest region, 10th in North America, and 33rd globally, with three availability zones served by the New Albany data center infrastructure.

On May 4, 2023, Google announced it would build two additional data centers in Columbus and Lancaster, Ohio, expanding beyond its existing New Albany campus to create a trio of Central Ohio facilities.

On August 29, 2023, Google announced a $1.7 billion investment to support its three Central Ohio data center campuses in New Albany, Columbus, and Lancaster, bringing cumulative Ohio investment to over $3.7 billion; each facility generates roughly 1,200 construction jobs and several hundred permanent positions.

On June 18, 2024, Google announced an additional $2.3 billion investment across its Columbus, New Albany, and Lancaster data center sites, bringing cumulative Ohio spending to over $4.4 billion since 2019.
In May 2025, Google subsidiary Montauk Innovations acquired an additional 85-acre parcel on Harrison Road Northwest in New Albany's business park in Licking County for $63 million.

On November 12, 2025, TotalEnergies announced a 15-year power purchase agreement to supply Google's Ohio data centers with 1.5 TWh of certified renewable electricity from the Montpelier solar farm in Ohio, connected to the PJM grid.

On April 2, 2026, the Ohio Ballot Board unanimously approved a petition drive for a constitutional amendment to ban new data centers consuming over 25 MW monthly, requiring 400,000+ signatures by July 2026; the campaign cited New Albany-area data center impacts including rising electric rates and farmland loss.

projects.name: Google Council Bluffs (East)

Google held a grand opening for its second Council Bluffs campus on Bunge Avenue, starting with 50 employees focused on installing, upgrading, and maintaining servers.

Google announced a third expansion phase (Southlands) in Council Bluffs, creating 35 additional positions and bringing total investment to $1.5 billion, the largest private investment in Iowa history at that time; the state increased Google's sales and use tax abatement from $9.6 million to $16.8 million.

Google announced a $350 million expansion of its Council Bluffs data center, the third expansion since 2007, along with a $250,000 grant to Advance Southwest Iowa; the campus then spanned over 2.5 million square feet east of Interstate 29 on Bunge Avenue.

Google announced an additional $1 billion investment in its Council Bluffs data center plus $1.3 million for water preservation in the Missouri River Valley Basin, bringing the campus to approximately 3 million square feet and total investment to over $6 billion.

Google announced a $7 billion investment in Iowa over the next two years for a new data center in Cedar Rapids and expansion of its existing Council Bluffs facility, plus a partnership with the Electrical Training Alliance to increase Iowa's electrical workforce pipeline by 95 percent.

Google and NextEra Energy announced a collaboration to restart the 615 MW Duane Arnold nuclear plant in Iowa under a 25-year power purchase agreement, with operations expected by Q1 2029, to support Google's expanding Iowa data center operations.

Google gave $3 million to Omaha's Metropolitan Utilities District to install acoustic leak detection sensors across 500 miles of high-priority water lines, part of a $17 million water stewardship initiative across seven states including Iowa where Google operates data centers.

The Council Bluffs City Council rejected Mayor Jill Shudak's proposed 12-month moratorium on new data center construction; Public Works Director Matt Cox noted data centers request one to two million gallons of water per day and individual projects could max out sewer capacity.

Flatwater Free Press reported that Google self-reported its Council Bluffs facility consumed 1.3 billion gallons of water in 2025, more than any of its other data center locations worldwide that year.

A construction apprentice was trapped under an elevator at Google Southlands in Council Bluffs and airlifted to a hospital after the Council Bluffs Fire Department extracted him; the incident occurred at approximately 5 p.m. during ongoing construction work.

projects.name: Google Lincoln
projects.note: Epoch AI estimates ~141 MW.

Google announced it will build its third data center in Nebraska, located north of Lincoln at the northwest corner of 56th Street and Interstate 80; the announcement was made at Google's Papillion campus with Rep. Mike Flood, Sen. Deb Fischer, and Lincoln Mayor Leirion Gaylor Baird present.

Governor Jim Pillen signed an executive order halting tax subsidies to large-scale data centers in Nebraska and established a data center task force to investigate environmental and water impacts; the article identifies the Google Lincoln facility at North 56th and Highway 77 as a $1.2 billion project with construction actively ongoing.

Google representatives and Lincoln city leaders discussed the data center's operational status; facility manager Jake Laney said a couple hundred workers are on site, and Chief Sustainability Officer Kim Morrow said the city is not looking to add any more data centers to Lincoln for the foreseeable future.

projects.name: Google Bristow

The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers approved Sharpless Enterprises' application for the 181-acre data center complex at 6201 Wellington Road near Bristow, after reviewing potential impacts on nearby wetlands and streams; Corps biologist Anna Lawston said nothing substantial changed between the initial application and final approval.

Google announced a $1 billion investment to expand its Virginia data centers, including its newly opened Prince William County campus and two Loudoun County sites, bringing total Virginia investment to over $4.2 billion; Governor Youngkin attended the announcement at Google's Reston headquarters.

Google announced an additional $9 billion investment in Virginia through the end of 2026 for cloud and AI infrastructure, including expansion of existing facilities in Prince William County; the Bristow Mango Farm complex is included in the investment, per the Prince William Times.

The Prince William Times reported that Google's Mango Farm data center complex at 13001 Rollins Ford Road in Bristow, next to Gainesville High School, occupies 250 acres with one operational data center of about 290,000 square feet, is valued at $1.2 billion by Prince William County, and has plans filed for at least two more data centers on the site.

Anthropic agreed to rent all computing capacity at SpaceX's Colossus 1, accessing over 220,000 Nvidia GPUs and more than 300 MW of AI compute; financial terms were not disclosed.
Google agreed to rent approximately 110,000 GPUs from SpaceX at Colossus 2 for $920 million monthly through June 2029, as reported by The New York Times.
The U.S. Department of Justice moved to intervene in and dismiss the NAACP's Clean Air Act lawsuit against xAI's Colossus data center gas turbines, as reported by The New York Times.

SpaceX agreed with the Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality to remove all 69 temporary mobile gas turbines at the Southaven power site by July 2027, with removal beginning as early as August 2026.

Governor Pillen signed an executive order suspending taxpayer-funded tax incentives for data centers and establishing a task force to identify safeguards protecting Nebraska's natural resources from data center operations.

KCUR reported Google's first KC-area campus near Worlds of Fun was still under construction and reportedly drawing roughly 1,000 construction workers.

Google and Keystone Community Corporation launched OnRamp, a two-part AI education initiative in Kansas City; the OnRamp Start cohort of 25 participants began May 5, 2026, with a youth-focused OnRamp Foundations track starting in June 2026.

projects.name: QTS Richmond 1

QTS announced it had invested $100 million in converting the former Qimonda site, with renovation about 5% complete and approximately 50 employees on site, projecting growth to 200 employees.

QTS announced it had acquired 200 additional acres at its Richmond Mega Data Center campus for expansion of up to 240 MW across 1.5 million sq ft of new capacity at White Oak Technology Park.

Henrico County's new provisional use permit (PUP) requirement for all hyperscale data centers took effect, including in White Oak Technology Park, requiring board-level approval for new facilities that previously could proceed by right in industrial zones.

The Henrico County Board of Supervisors approved new data center regulations including 500-foot tree buffers from residential areas, generator testing limits, mandatory equipment screening, and closed-loop cooling requirements; rules apply retroactively to rezoned projects without final site plan approval.

projects.name: Meta Rosemount

Rosemount City Council voted unanimously to approve Meta's data center, rezoning the 280-acre UMore Park parcel from agricultural to business park planned development.

Alpha News reported that Rosemount approved Meta's 750,000-sq-ft data center despite residents' concerns about soil contaminants from the site's WWII munitions history, 24/7 low-frequency noise, and water usage during local restrictions; the filing entity is Jimnist LLC.

Meta acquired another 14-acre plot off Blaine Avenue East near 145th Street in Rosemount for $5 million via subsidiary Jimnist, bringing total known land holdings to at least 494 acres.

Meta and Amrize deployed an AI-optimized concrete mix (BOxCrete) for the Rosemount data center foundation, achieving full structural strength 43% faster and reducing cracking risk by nearly 10%; the mix was qualified for additional areas of the facility.
Rosemount halted new data center proposals with a moratorium, pausing discussion of additional facilities beyond Meta's already-approved project.
InForum reported that Minnesota's first hyperscale data center is nearing completion in Rosemount.

projects.name: Amazon Madison Mega Site

AWS's Project Rainier — the AI training cluster powering Anthropic's Claude, spread across Pennsylvania, Indiana, and Mississippi — was reported operational, with its Mississippi campus near Canton in Madison County cited at more than 350 MW of IT capacity and set to ramp past 1 GW.

Canton residents described construction dust, noise and pollution fears; Madison County constable Johnny Sims said construction dust had worsened his teenage daughter's asthma, and Amazon stated it is committed to being a responsible community partner.

Of Amazon four announced Mississippi data center facilities, the Canton campus in Madison County was reported as the one currently operating, with more than 700 diesel generators planned across the two Madison County campuses and the Canton facility set to transition to 100% recycled wastewater for cooling by 2027.

projects.name: Microsoft Goodyear

events.summary: Microsoft purchased 279 acres in Goodyear from Carefree Partners Investments for $48 million, land later used for its data center campus south of I-10 and Phoenix Goodyear Airport.
Goodyear City Council approved rezoning of Microsoft's parcel from final planned area development to I-1 (light industrial park) with a PAD overlay (December 2018).

projects.name: Google Lancaster

events.summary: Google announced Lancaster as the site for a future data center on Whiley Road in the Rock Mill Industrial Park; the city's Economic Development Director Mike Pettit had worked over a year to secure the project, and Google purchased approximately 120 acres of farmland for close to $4 million in August 2021.

Google formally announced construction of two new data centers in Columbus and Lancaster, bringing its total Ohio investment to over $2 billion; Lancaster Mayor David Scheffler confirmed a 15-year, 100% tax abatement on real estate improvements, buildings, and equipment, plus a $700,000 roadwork grant from the Ohio Department of Development.

Construction began on Google's Lancaster campus at 104 Whiley Road on approximately 120 acres, with union labor from the Columbus/Central Ohio Building and Construction Trades Council (over 18,000 workers across 21 affiliated local unions); Google also awarded a $100,000 grant to the Columbus Building Futures Program.

Ohio Governor Mike DeWine and Google VP of Government Affairs Mark Isakowitz announced the two new central Ohio data centers; Isakowitz stated Google would have three operational data centers in central Ohio, and the $120 million Lancaster campus was described as being built on roughly 120 acres of farmland.

Google announced an additional $1.7 billion investment across its three central Ohio data center campuses in Columbus, New Albany, and Lancaster, to complete the Columbus and Lancaster centers and expand New Albany; each center was estimated to create approximately 1,200 construction jobs and a few hundred permanent employees.

Construction Dive reported Google's $1.7 billion investment across its three Ohio campuses, with Ohio Lt. Gov. Jon Husted stating that Ohio is establishing itself as a premier destination for technology investment.
The first data center building on Google's Lancaster campus was completed and became operational in 2024, according to Baxtel's facility tracker.

Google announced a further $2.3 billion investment in its three Ohio data center campuses (Columbus, New Albany, and Lancaster), bringing total Ohio investment to over $4.4 billion since 2019; Lt. Gov. Jon Husted called central Ohio an important tech hub.
A second building on Google's Lancaster campus (designated Lancaster 2 / 'Core Plaza') was completed and became operational in 2025, according to Baxtel's facility tracker.

A Governing.com investigation confirmed Google has a Community Reinvestment Area (CRA) agreement with Lancaster but Google declined to disclose the specific terms; a related Google subsidiary (Magellan Enterprises LLC) received a 100%, 15-year CRA in Columbus valued at $54 million for 20 projected jobs.

Google signed a 15-year power purchase agreement with TotalEnergies for 1.5 TWh of renewable electricity from TotalEnergies' 49 MW Montpelier solar farm in Ohio, connected to the PJM grid to support Google's Ohio data center operations including Lancaster.

projects.name: Google Mesa
projects.note: Chip types: TPU v6e. Epoch AI estimates ~90 MW.

events.summary: Mesa rezoned approximately 187 acres of Morrison family farmland at Elliot and Sossaman roads for the data center project, then known by the codename Project Red Hawk, in April 2019.

Mesa City Council approved a development agreement and 25-year Government Property Lease Excise Tax (GPLET) incentive for Google's $1 billion data center on 187 acres at Elliot and Sossaman roads; the deal was negotiated under the codename Project Red Hawk with Google operating as Stone Applications LLC.

AZBEX reported the council approval and revealed Google as the company behind Project Red Hawk, noting the project had been secret for over a year due to a confidentiality agreement; Mayor Giles said the corridor would be anchored by Apple and Google.

Mesa Design Review Board began reviewing the Phase 1 site plan for the 288,530-square-foot data center building, utility switchyard, medium-voltage substation, security kiosk, and employee office building; engineering firm HDR Inc. submitted the plans on behalf of Stone Applications LLC.

Google broke ground on its $600 million Phase 1 data center in Mesa, its first physical presence in Arizona; Governor Katie Hobbs, Mayor John Giles, and Rep. Greg Stanton attended; Google announced the facility would be 100% air-cooled and donated $150,000 to Salt River Project for watershed restoration.

Construction Dive reported on Google's $600 million Mesa data center groundbreaking, noting it was Google's first physical presence in Arizona and that a new Google Cloud region was also coming to Phoenix.

Mesa Tribune reported that city officials were looking to slow data center growth, with Councilman Scott Somers saying Mesa had seen 'more than our fair share' of data centers; at least 15 new data center projects were reportedly eyeing Mesa, and Google's $600 million facility was noted alongside the city's concerns about low job creation per acre.

Mesa Design Review Board heard informational presentations on Google's Phase 2 data center (280,000 sq ft, air-cooled, codenamed Project Redhawk) and a separate one-story Redhawk HUB office building near Elliot and Sossaman roads; no formal action was taken.

ABC15 reported that Google's Phase 2 design review was underway for a 280,000-square-foot building mirroring Phase 1, plus a Redhawk-HUB office building, on the campus that now represented a total $1 billion investment on over 185 acres.
Google's Phase 1 data center (288,530 sq ft) at the Red Hawk campus in Mesa became operational in July 2025, powered by air-cooling architecture with no water-intensive cooling towers.

Mesa City Council adopted new data center zoning regulations establishing 'Data Center' as a distinct land use category, after 15 data centers were constructed, approved, or proposed in the city over six years; Vice Mayor Somers called it the first step in more objective design standards.

Mesa Design Review Board examined Phase 3 plans for a 283,500-square-foot data center building at 35 feet 10 inches tall with two server halls, including alternative compliance requests for wall and roof articulations under the Mesa Zoning Ordinance.

projects.name: Meta-QTS Hillsboro 2
projects.note: Chip types: H100. Epoch AI estimates ~180 MW.

events.summary: QTS announced commencement of development on its 92-acre mega data center campus in Hillsboro, Oregon, planning five buildings totaling over 1 million leasable sq ft and 250+ MW gross power capacity.
QTS opened Phase 1 of its Hillsboro campus, a 158,000 sq ft, 24 MW data center, with 100% of the first phase pre-leased to a global SaaS provider at approximately 4.5 MW.

Blackstone announced an all-cash acquisition of QTS Realty Trust at $78 per share (approximately $10 billion including debt), the largest data center M&A deal at the time; the deal was expected to close later in 2021.

In September 2021, Portland General Electric and QTS jointly filed with the Oregon Public Utility Commission seeking approval to expand PGE's renewable energy program by 250 MW of new renewable resources to support Facebook's anticipated usage at the fully expanded QTS Hillsboro campus.

Data Center Frontier reported that Meta secured a 35 MW lease at QTS's Hillsboro campus as part of its 2021 leasing activity, with QTS seeking up to 250 MW of power from PGE to support Facebook's anticipated expansion.

In May 2022, CBRE reported 199 MW of pre-leasing in the Hillsboro data center market entering 2022, with the bulk going to one large social media company (Meta) at a single facility (QTS), and QTS planning to deploy 200 MW of IT capacity at the campus.

Avangrid, PGE, QTS, and Meta announced a PPA for Tower Solar, a 120 MWac (166 MWdc) solar project in Morrow County, Oregon, to supply clean energy through PGE's Green Future Impact program supporting QTS and Meta's data center operations.

KLCC reported that Oregon data centers use 11% of the state's electricity, potentially doubling to 25% within 3-4 years, with Hillsboro identified as a key hub where industrial land has become scarce due to rapid data center development.

The Hillsboro Herald published an open letter citing $11 billion in data center tax breaks extended through 2051 and linking the city's $1.6 billion water infrastructure debt to System Development Charges tied to data center growth; over 3,400 signatures had been gathered on a moratorium petition.

Approximately 100 Hillsboro residents rallied at Shute Farm to oppose data center tax giveaways; speakers cited $67 million in annual exempted property taxes from four nearby data centers, with QTS facilities holding a $2.428 billion exemption, and a moratorium petition nearing 4,000 signatures.

About 40 Hillsboro residents spoke at a June 2 City Council meeting demanding a halt to data center development, citing concerns over farmland consumption (470 acres), water and energy costs, noise, and limited job creation; Council President Rob Harris proposed considering a one-year moratorium.

1000 Friends of Oregon and the Oregon Education Association filed suit challenging multiple enterprise zone tax exemption agreements for data center projects (including QTS) approved in spring 2026 before Oregon's statewide moratorium took effect on June 6.

The Hillsboro City Council unanimously voted to impose a 120-day moratorium on new data center and battery energy storage system applications, including expansions, effective until at least November 24, 2026.

projects.name: Google Red Oak
projects.note: Chip types: TPU v6e,TPU v7. Epoch AI estimates ~77 MW.

events.summary: Google announced a new data center campus in Red Oak, Texas, its second site in Ellis County after Midlothian, with at least $600 million planned investment over multiple years and $330 million committed for 2023; the project was expected to create nearly 1,200 construction jobs and 30 permanent positions.

Google awarded a $150,000 grant to Red Oak ISD to fund STEM expansion including Project Lead the Way engineering, robotics, and science initiatives at secondary schools, announced alongside the data center campus.

Dallas Innovates reported Google's $600 million Red Oak data center would complement its existing Midlothian facility and the Dallas cloud region, with VP of Government Affairs Cris Turner stating the infrastructure supports AI innovations and Google Cloud business.
Google awarded $100,000 grants each to the Red Oak and Midlothian public libraries; Red Oak's grant funded a makerspace with 3D printers and robotics technology for community STEM exploration.

Google announced over $1 billion in Texas investment for 2024, targeting the Midlothian and Red Oak data center campuses, bringing its total Texas investment past $2.7 billion; the company also announced 375 MW of carbon-free solar power purchase agreements for ERCOT.

As part of a $40 billion Texas investment announcement through 2027, Google disclosed that the first building of its Red Oak campus in Ellis County is now operational; the broader plan includes new campuses in Armstrong, Haskell, and Wilbarger counties plus over 6,200 MW of new energy generation.

projects.name: Meta Gallatin
projects.note: Chip types: B300. Epoch AI estimates ~87 MW.

events.summary: Woolhawk LLC (later revealed as Facebook) acquired 809 acres in Gallatin for approximately $15-20 million for a planned data center campus; the project was referred to as 'Project Woolhawk' by local officials.

Gallatin's Industrial Development Board advanced a PILOT (payment in lieu of taxes) agreement for Woolhawk LLC with 20-year tax abatement terms starting at $1 million per year for the first building and decreasing to $550,000 for the sixth building.

Facebook announced an $800 million, 982,000-square-foot data center in Gallatin, Tennessee, culminating a three-year recruitment effort by the Gallatin EDA and TVA; the facility would support approximately 100 permanent jobs.

Facebook confirmed the Gallatin data center as its 13th in the U.S., revealing the 809-acre site was purchased under Woolhawk LLC for $20 million and that the city approved $19.5 million in tax breaks; the first building was expected in approximately two years with a second 18 months later.

Facebook broke ground on the Gallatin data center campus, with DPR Construction as general contractor; the facility was designed to use 80% less water than an average data center, achieve LEED Gold certification, and run on 100% renewable energy.
Facebook announced it had signed contracts for 220 MW of new solar energy generation in Tennessee through a partnership with TVA to support the Gallatin data center.
Data Center Frontier reported the Gallatin project as Facebook's third data center announcement since the COVID-19 pandemic began, following DeKalb, Illinois and Prineville, Oregon expansions.

Meta announced a nearly $1 billion expansion of the Gallatin campus with two new structures totaling approximately 2 million square feet, including a cold storage facility, with peak construction workforce reaching 1,700 workers.
Meta's first data center building on the Gallatin campus became fully operational in 2023, designated GTN 1, a two-story H-shaped building on 800 acres at 1 Meta Loop.

Meta filed plans for a fourth data center on its Gallatin campus, a 278,000-square-foot building shaped like a stretched plus sign representing a 17% increase to its existing footprint, with a public work session set for April 29 and a vote scheduled for May 20, 2024.

Gallatin approved Meta's fourth data center building on the campus, a 276,000-square-foot structure that would bring total campus space to approximately 1.9 million square feet with total investment well beyond $1 billion.

Meta officially launched its Gallatin data center campus as operational, with total investment exceeding $1.5 billion across four buildings totaling more than 1.7 million square feet and over 100 permanent employees; the Nashville Business Journal called it one of the top five largest business investments in Tennessee history.

The Tennessee Municipal League reported Meta's Gallatin data center began operations, noting the company's partnership with TVA supports eight Meta projects adding 530 MW of renewable energy to Tennessee and that Meta had donated over $1 million to local nonprofits and school systems.

projects.name: Meta Los Lunas
projects.note: Chip types: B300. Epoch AI estimates ~87 MW.

events.summary: Facebook announced plans to build a new data center in Los Lunas, New Mexico, its seventh overall and fifth in the U.S., to be powered by 100% renewable energy.
New Mexico's congressional delegation welcomed the Facebook data center announcement; senators and representatives had previously written to the PRC advocating for Los Lunas as the site.

The Los Lunas Village Council had approved an up-to-$30 billion industrial revenue bond proposal in late June 2016 under the codename 'Greater Kudu' without initially knowing Facebook's involvement; the project also used codenames 'Project Antelope' and 'Project Discus' during a competitive process with Utah.
Facebook held a groundbreaking ceremony at the Huning Business Park in Los Lunas, attended by Governor Susana Martinez and Mayor Charles Griego, beginning the $250 million Phase 1 construction.

Facebook opened its Los Lunas data center campus, initially supporting over 150 jobs, with the facility pursuing LEED v4 Gold certification and backed by over 396 MW of new wind and solar resources on the New Mexico grid.

Facebook announced a two-building, $800 million expansion of the Los Lunas campus, bringing total investment to nearly $2 billion and projected employment to over 400 operational jobs, with a new goal to restore 200% of water consumed to New Mexico watersheds.

Facebook announced the two new buildings would form an H-shape on the southern end of the 750-acre campus, with each data hall housing 3,200 servers; ground preparation by Fortis was underway with foundation construction to begin January 2022 and first building turnover targeted for October 2024.

The $800 million expansion was reported to bring total investment to $2.2 billion, expand the campus to nearly 3.8 million square feet across eight buildings, and employ over 1,000 construction workers with more than 70% New Mexico subcontractors.

The Los Lunas Village Council unanimously approved a resolution declaring intent to issue up to six series of IRBs not exceeding $7.5 billion each for Greater Kudu LLC (Meta subsidiary) to build two new AI-dedicated buildings for $800 million, with construction expected to begin spring 2025 and take 2-3 years.

The Los Lunas Village Council unanimously approved an IRB ordinance for Greater Kudu LLC and unanimously approved an amended water agreement capping daily use at 3 million gallons (reduced from 4.5 million), removing the data center's previous priority status during shortages, and keeping the annual allocation at 500 acre-feet.
The Los Lunas Village Council approved a project partnership with tax incentives requiring Meta to invest $350 million in the expansion within 10 years of the agreement.

Meta acquired a 474-acre parcel adjacent to its existing Los Lunas data center campus at $128,500 per acre, brokered by CBRE, within the Huning Business and Tech Park for next-generation data center facilities.

projects.name: CoreWeave Ellendale ND
projects.note: Chip types: B200. Epoch AI estimates ~68 MW.

events.summary: Applied Blockchain (now Applied Digital) broke ground on a 180 MW data center facility in Ellendale, North Dakota (Dickey County), its second North Dakota site, with a five-year Energy Service Agreement signed with a local utility on September 1, 2022.

Applied Digital announced the energization of its 180 MW Ellendale facility, completed six months after groundbreaking; Marathon Digital Holdings contracted for capacity with an option for an additional 70 MW, and the project was financed through a $20 million loan from Starion Bank.

Applied Digital held a ribbon-cutting ceremony celebrating the energization of its 180 MW Ellendale facility, attended by local congressional and state representatives; the company received final regulatory approval from the North Dakota Public Service Commission for its Electric Service Agreement.

Applied Digital broke ground on a separate 100 MW, 342,000-square-foot HPC facility at the Ellendale campus designed for AI workloads including generative AI and machine learning, with capacity for nearly 50,000 Nvidia H100 SXM-class GPUs in a liquid-cooled configuration.

Applied Digital signed a conditional anchor tenant agreement at the Ellendale HPC facility for 100 MW over 10 years valued at approximately $2.2 billion, pending finalization of definitive lease documents and construction financing.

Applied Digital extended the 45-day negotiation period for the conditional anchor tenant agreement at the Ellendale HPC facility until March 30, 2024, with the 100 MW, 10-year deal still under negotiation.

Applied Digital issued a $50 million unsecured convertible debenture to a single private investor with a 54-week term and no interest payments, with proceeds directed toward construction of the Ellendale HPC data center.
Applied Digital issued a $42.1 million unsecured convertible debenture to advance construction of the Ellendale HPC data center, with a 54-week term, no interest, and a 5% original issue discount.
Applied Digital secured a $125 million debt facility (expandable to $200 million) from CIM Group at 12% annual interest for a 3-year term, exclusively for buildout of the Ellendale HPC campus.

Applied Digital announced the successful energization of the on-site main substation transformer at the Ellendale HPC campus, enabling equipment commissioning; the company also submitted a petition for property annexation to the City of Ellendale and received the Community Impact award at the 18th Annual Data Center Dynamics Awards.

Applied Digital closed a $375 million interim financing with Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation (SMBC) to repay a Macquarie Capital note and fund development of the first and second buildings at the Ellendale HPC campus.

Applied Digital entered into a $150 million convertible preferred equity facility with institutional investors to advance development of the Ellendale multi-building HPC campus, with draws at company discretion in $25 million increments over a 36-month term.

Applied Digital announced a 250 MW AI data center lease with CoreWeave at the Ellendale campus for approximately 15 years, with an optional 150 MW expansion to 400 MW total; the first 100 MW building expected operational in Q4 2025 and the second 150 MW building by mid-2026, with anticipated total revenue of approximately $7 billion.

Applied Digital finalized an additional 150 MW lease with CoreWeave at the Polaris Forge 1 campus in Ellendale, bringing total contracted capacity to 400 MW across three lease agreements with approximately 15-year terms and total anticipated revenue of approximately $11 billion.

Applied Digital achieved Ready for Service for Phase 1 (50 MW) of the first 100 MW building at Polaris Forge 1 in Ellendale for CoreWeave, featuring proprietary liquid cooling with near-zero water consumption.

Applied Digital priced $1.59 billion in 7.000% senior secured notes due 2031 to fund construction of the fourth 150 MW building (ELN-04) at Polaris Forge 1 in Ellendale and repay a Goldman Sachs bridge loan.

Applied Digital delivered Building 2 Phase 1 at Polaris Forge 1 in Ellendale, adding 75 MW and bringing total live campus capacity to 175 MW (100 MW from Building 1 plus 75 MW from Building 2), on schedule toward the 400 MW contracted total.

projects.name: Meta Sarpy
projects.note: Chip types: B300. Epoch AI estimates ~80 MW.

events.summary: Meta's info sheet states the company broke ground on the Sarpy Data Center in 2017, with a total investment of over $2.5 billion in Nebraska.

Facebook announced an expansion of its Sarpy County data center campus to approximately 3.6 million square feet across 8 buildings on roughly 500 acres, with total investment at that time of approximately $1.5 billion and a 2024 completion target.
Meta announced it was adding a ninth facility to the Sarpy Data Center campus in Springfield; county records showed Meta pays $3.8 million in property taxes between two parcels of land.

Construction was halted at the Meta data center in Sarpy County after racist graffiti was found on site for a recurring time, with contractor Turner Construction stopping work at the $1.5 billion project.

projects.name: CoreWeave Chester VA
projects.note: Chip types: H100,B200. Epoch AI estimates ~82 MW.

events.summary: Chirisa Technology Parks offers the former Capital One data center in Virginia to hyperscaler tenants, per Data Center Dynamics.
Chirisa secures a $200 million loan to fit out the Virginia data center for CoreWeave, per Data Center Dynamics.

Chirisa announces 150 MW of expansion across U.S. sites including a 300 MW substation and up to 1 million sq ft at the former Capital One campus in Meadowville Technology Park, Chesterfield County; Chesterfield Board Chairman Jim Holland praises the campus transformation.
Chirisa plans a 20 MW data center in Chesterfield County, Virginia, per Data Center Dynamics.
Chirisa announces senior hires to lead hyperscale build-to-suit delivery, citing its CTP-01 data center in Chesterfield, VA and a pipeline exceeding 600 MW under development.

Blue Owl Capital, Chirisa, and PowerHouse Data Centers announce the first phase of a $5 billion joint venture with CoreWeave as anchor customer for an initial 120 MW on Chirisa's 350-acre campus near Richmond, Virginia, for 2025-2026 delivery.
Chirisa and PowerHouse plan a 1 GW data center campus outside Richmond, Virginia, per Data Center Dynamics.

A Societe Generale-led syndicate closes a $600 million construction loan for a 50 MW build-to-suit data center preleased to CoreWeave at the 300-plus-acre Chirisa Technology Park near Richmond; the project broke ground in 2024.
A fire is contained inside the Chirisa data center in Chesterfield County; WRIC ABC 8News reports questions remain about the incident.
A second fire in three weeks occurs at the Chirisa data center in Chesterfield County, Virginia, per Data Center Dynamics.
After four fires in 12 months at its Chesterfield data center, Chirisa blames defective batteries as the root cause, per The Progress Index.

Chirisa and American Real Estate Partners plan two new 100 MW data center buildings (380,000 sq ft total) at 1600 Digital Drive on the former Cartograf site in Chesterfield County, acquired for $16.5 million; CoreWeave will operate inside the data halls, with the first building targeted for late 2027.

projects.name: AWS Berwick
projects.note: Part of Project Rainier. Chip types: Trainium2. Epoch AI estimates ~108 MW.

events.summary: AWS acquired Talen Energy's Cumulus Data campus adjacent to the Susquehanna nuclear power station in Salem Township, Luzerne County, PA for $650 million ($350M at closing, $300M at milestones), gaining access to a 960 MW data center campus directly connected to the 2,520 MW nuclear plant.
AWS was granted a 1,600-acre rezoning request and announced plans for a 15-building data center campus at the Pennsylvania nuclear site in Salem Township.

FERC voted 2-1 to reject PJM's proposed interconnection agreement that would have expanded Amazon's co-located data center load at Susquehanna from 300 MW to 480 MW, citing concerns about cost fairness and grid reliability precedent.
FERC upheld its rejection of the proposed interconnection agreement between AWS's data center and the Susquehanna nuclear plant, denying Talen Energy's rehearing request.

Governor Shapiro announced at a Berwick event that Amazon plans to invest at least $20 billion in Pennsylvania data centers, the largest private-sector investment in state history, with Salem Township (Luzerne County) and Falls Township (Bucks County) as the first two identified sites, creating at least 1,250 jobs.

Talen Energy and AWS announced a restructured 17-year, $18 billion power purchase agreement for up to 1,920 MW from Susquehanna nuclear station, converting the behind-the-meter arrangement to a grid-connected front-of-the-meter model to comply with FERC's ruling, with full volume delivery by 2032.
Amazon reported that data center campus construction in Salem Township was proceeding at a rapid pace.

Nonprofit Quarterly published an investigative feature titled 'A Canary in a Coal Mine: Amazon's Luzerne County Data Center,' examining community and environmental concerns including energy demand, water quality, tax exemptions, and employment claims.

The Susquehanna River Basin Commission approved an increase in consumptive water use for the Amazon data center in Salem Township from 60,000 to 129,000 gallons per day (reduced from the initial request of 277,000 gpd), sourced from PA American Water (Berwick).
Blackstone-owned QTS spent $580 million to acquire land in Salem Township for a separate data center campus adjacent to the Amazon site, with plans for 12 to 17 data centers.

96 Salem Township landowners completed a historic 1,700-acre land sale to QTS for more than $500 million for a major data center campus adjacent to the Amazon site, with Salem Township receiving a $9 million community benefit agreement.
WNEP reported that the community of Salem Township is now encircled by new data center developments, with multiple campuses under construction or planned in the area.
Amazon donated $250,000 to the Bloomsburg Area YMCA for a new STEM lab as data center construction near Berwick continued.
The Citizens' Voice reported that a third data center in Salem Township could generate $1.2 billion for landowners, reflecting the scale of data center land acquisition in the area.
The Center Square reported on the role of big money and enforced silence (NDAs) in Pennsylvania's data center push, covering the Salem Township/Amazon development.
Salem Township paused new data center projects pending a zoning amendment, responding to community concerns about the pace of development.
State representatives were denied access to the Amazon data center in Salem Township, as reported by the Citizens' Voice.

PA DEP published notice inviting public comments (deadline September 14, 2026) on an air quality permit for 84 backup diesel generators, 2 auxiliary emergency generators, and fuel storage tanks for an expansion of the existing Amazon data center in Salem Township.

projects.name: Google Papillion
projects.note: Chip types: TPU v4,TPU v5e,TPU v6e,TPU v5p. Epoch AI estimates ~237 MW.

events.summary: Data Center Dynamics reports that a project code-named 'Project Wizard' in Sarpy County has evidence pointing to Google as the developer of a major new data center.

Google holds a groundbreaking ceremony for a $600 million data center on a 275-acre site off Highway 50 and Schram Road in Papillion, with Governor Pete Ricketts, Congressman Don Bacon, and Mayor David Black in attendance; the facility is described as Google's 13th nationwide.

KMTV reports that OPPD had been collaborating with Google on power infrastructure for approximately six years prior to the groundbreaking, and Google expects the Papillion facility to be operational within 18-24 months.

Google announces at least $750 million in new Nebraska investment including expansion of its Papillion campus at 14706 Schram Road (then employing 120 people) and a new data center in northwest Omaha, bringing total state investment past $1 billion.

Google announces $1.2 billion in new Nebraska investment to expand the Papillion and Omaha facilities and build a third data center in Lincoln; the Papillion facility is described as having created over 120 jobs since opening in 2019.

In November 2025, Silicon Prairie News reports that OPPD now anticipates annual electricity demand growth of over 100 MW (up from 4 MW previously), driven by data center expansion including Google's Sarpy County facility described as its first in Nebraska.

Google announces $17 million in water stewardship grants across seven states; the Metropolitan Utilities District in Omaha receives $3 million for acoustic leak-detection sensors across 500 miles of water lines, tied to Google's three Nebraska data centers.

In July 2026, Flatwater Free Press reports that Google's Nebraska data centers consumed approximately 732 million gallons of water in 2025, up from 46.6 million gallons in 2022 and 134.7 million gallons in 2023; the Papillion facility is identified as one of three sites.

Grist reports that Nebraska passed a law requiring data centers to disclose annual water consumption and power demand to the Department of Water, Energy, and Environment; Google's three Nebraska facilities including Papillion consumed approximately 732 million gallons in 2025.
Governor Pillen signs an executive order curbing tax incentives for large data centers; KOLN reports that Nebraska data centers have received $519 million in property tax exemptions since 2021.

projects.name: CoreWeave Marble NC
projects.note: Chip types: B200. Epoch AI estimates ~65 MW.
