Topeka City Council held a special meeting where Compass and Evergy presented and fielded 90 minutes of questions on the proposed 400-MW-class project; Mayor confirmed the city moratorium remains in effect.
Topeka Planning Commission discussed a proposed text amendment creating specific zoning standards for data centers (including hyperscale facilities), prompted by the Compass proposal.

projects.name: DataBank Project Indo
projects.note: 200MW, $2.4B, 1.1M sq ft data center campus at 218 Industrial Park Road near Atlanta; filed a Development of Regional Impact application and a 288MW grid interconnection request.

events.summary: DataBank Holdings filed a Development of Regional Impact (DRI) application with the Georgia Department of Community Affairs for 'Project Indo,' a proposed 200 MW data center campus on 69 acres at 218 Industrial Park Road, Cartersville, seeking a 288 MW utility grid connection; full build-out is estimated at $2.4 billion with first phase targeted for 2032.

DataBank filed a rezoning request with the City of Cartersville to change the 218 Industrial Park Road site from HI (heavy industrial) to T (technology district) to permit the ~1 million-sq-ft data center and on-site power substation; city planner David Hardegree said the request would go before the Planning Commission on August 11, with projected annual tax revenue of $23 million and 60 full-time jobs.

Northwest Georgia News reported further details on Project Indo, including a DRI-estimated water use of roughly 5,082 gallons per day; Bartow County Administrator Peter Olson and Commissioner Steve Taylor downplayed traffic and water impacts and framed the project as a tax-revenue benefit for the county.
Cartersville Planning Commission scheduled hearing on DataBank's rezoning request (HI to Technology district) for the Project Indo data center campus at 218 Industrial Park Road.

projects.name: Aligned Shippingport (Project Phoenix)
projects.note: Nearly 2M sq ft, ~$10B natural-gas-powered data center campus on the former Bruce Mansfield coal plant site; land deal ($223.15M) closed July 29, 2026.

events.summary: Frontier Group acquired the former Bruce Mansfield coal-fired power plant site (660 acres) from Energy Harbor Corp, cleared coal piles, and began marketing the property as Shippingport Industrial Park.
Shippingport Borough solicitor began drafting the borough initial data-center zoning ordinance in anticipation of large-scale proposals at the former Bruce Mansfield site.
Shippingport Borough Council passed a new data-center zoning ordinance establishing use and permitting rules ahead of Aligned formal application.
A Vistra subsidiary purchased a 74-acre farm in nearby Hookstown for $4.2 million, underscoring the broader wave of AI/data-center-driven land acquisition around Shippingport and Beaver Valley.

Residents and officials raised transparency concerns about Frontier Group plans at a Shippingport borough meeting, prompting Gov. Shapiro to later say too many such projects have been shrouded in secrecy.
BlackRock led a roughly $40 billion deal to acquire Aligned Data Centers, the developer behind the proposed Shippingport Project Phoenix campus.
Aligned Data Centers filed a conditional-use application with Shippingport Borough for Project Phoenix on the former Bruce Mansfield power plant site.
Aligned held its first public information meeting in Shippingport to present Project Phoenix to residents; a company representative apologized for confusion surrounding the proposal.

Shippingport Borough Council approved most of Aligned conditional-use permit for up to three data center buildings totaling roughly 2 million square feet plus an on-site natural gas power plant; only about four residents attended.

Coverage detailed Aligned roughly $10 billion Shippingport Industrial Park campus plan on the ~660-acre former Bruce Mansfield site, with conditional use permits approved and the project in pre-construction planning.

Pittsburgh Post-Gazette reported Beaver Valley becoming a regional data-center target, noting Aligned natural gas plan alongside a separate Vistra-Meta power purchase agreement tied to the Beaver Valley nuclear plant.

Detailed site-plan figures: 593 acres, three two-story buildings up to 59 feet tall (1.95 million sq ft combined), a 70-acre natural gas power-generation pad, and 250 parking spaces; six parcels still needed acquisition.

Aligned/Frontier applied for mass grading, NPDES, and stormwater permits plus variances for 59-ft building height, up to 75% woodland clearing, 65-dB operational noise limits, and round-the-clock construction noise.

Frontier Group plan to convert adjacent former Bruce Mansfield coal units to natural gas generation (up to 3.6 GW, ~$3.2 billion via EQT and National Fuel Gas) cited as the eventual power source for the Aligned campus.

Mixed local reaction: some welcomed jobs while Beaver County economic development president cautioned that blindly chasing data centers is not the way to go; residents cited property-value and mine-subsidence concerns.

Pennsylvania House voted 197-5 to pass HB 2198 repealing the state Computer Data Center Equipment sales-tax incentive program, projected to cost $188.4 million in FY2026-27 growing to $517 million by 2030.
Aligned Data Centers closed its purchase of 650.89 acres in Shippingport from Frontier Group for $223,150,865 to build its nearly 2-million-square-foot data center campus.

projects.name: Talen Energy Montour Data Center
projects.note: County commissioners unanimously denied Talen Energy's request to rezone 800+ acres from agricultural to industrial for a data center plus power-plant expansion, after a grassroots group gathered ~3,000 petition signatures.

events.summary: FERC rejected a proposed interconnection service agreement among PJM, PPL Electric, and Talen that would have increased the load Talen could transfer directly from the Susquehanna nuclear plant to its co-located Amazon data center campus.

Talen Energy expanded its Amazon Web Services partnership with a new long-term agreement to supply up to 1,920 MWe from its Susquehanna nuclear plant through 2042, part of Talen's broader co-location strategy for AI data centers in Pennsylvania.
Concerned Citizens of Montour County formed with four members after Talen's rezoning request became public; its first town hall days later drew about 120 people.

Talen Energy submitted a rezoning petition to Montour County covering roughly 870 acres in Anthony and Derry Townships, seeking to change land from agricultural to industrial near its Montour Steam Electric Station for a data center and power-plant expansion.
The Montour County Planning Commission voted to recommend against Talen Energy's request to rezone roughly 870 acres of agricultural land to industrial.

Montour County commissioners held an all-day public hearing at First Baptist Church of Danville on Talen's rezoning request; residents wearing red 'Say No Industrial Rezoning' shirts testified about farmland loss, water use, noise, and land impact.

Concerned Citizens of Montour County delivered a petition signed by about 3,000 residents opposing the rezoning, roughly twice the population of the township and more than voted there in the 2024 election.

Montour County's three commissioners voted unanimously to deny Talen Energy's rezoning request; Chair Rebecca Dressler said Talen had not met its burden of proving the project would benefit the community and that no evidence showed benefits outweighed foreseeable public harms.

Talen Energy responded saying it remains committed to pursuing a data center in Montour County and would 'listen, incorporate feedback from the Commissioners, engage with the community, and refine our plans.'
Civil Eats profiled the Montour County fight as a case study of a small farm county organizing successfully against a hyperscale data center and power-plant expansion.
Montour County held a public hearing on proposed amendments to its data center ordinance, including new height and setback distance requirements.
Montour County commissioners unanimously approved amended data center ordinance provisions establishing new height and setback requirements for any future data center development.

Governor Josh Shapiro signed an executive order restricting data center development in Pennsylvania, eliminating fast-tracked permitting and formalizing GRID Standards requiring community engagement, energy-affordability protections, and environmental standards for developers seeking state support.

projects.name: Flexential Kaufman County
projects.note: Fourth and largest Flexential DFW-area facility; 110-acre site supports up to three 36MW buildings (108MW total); Phase 1 is 375,000 sq ft / 36MW, site work starting early 2027.

events.summary: The Flexential project site near Talty was released from the City of Talty extraterritorial jurisdiction (ETJ) under Texas state law after a petition was filed with Kaufman County, leaving Talty with no regulatory authority over the site.
Data Center Dynamics reported Flexential acquisition of 110 acres outside Dallas for a planned 108 MW campus, noting the design targets closed-loop cooling with zero water usage.

Flexential announced it purchased 110 acres in Kaufman County near Talty to build its fourth and largest Dallas-area data center campus, with Phase 1 comprising a 375,000 sq ft, 36 MW building and full build-out potential of 108 MW across three buildings.

Connect CRE reported Flexential land acquisition for a 375,000 sq ft, 36 MW first-phase data center about 20 minutes east of Dallas in Talty, citing Cushman and Wakefield ranking of Dallas as the world top data center market.
Unite.AI reported Flexential had secured 36 MW of power for the first building — exceeding the combined electrical capacity of its three existing Dallas-area facilities (28.4 MW).

Local press reported Talty officials say the city has no regulatory authority over the Flexential site because the property was released from the city ETJ earlier in 2026 after a Kaufman County petition.

projects.name: Iron Mountain Hutto Campus
projects.note: Seven-building data center campus proposed outside Austin near the Samsung Taylor plant, with on-site substation; exploring behind-the-meter natural gas to speed up power availability.

events.summary: Iron Mountain presented the proposed seven-building Taylor Meadows data center campus (~500 acres off FM 3349) to Hutto City Council, requesting wastewater service (~30,200 gallons/day). City Manager said the city would require substantial community benefits in exchange for service.

Iron Mountain offered Hutto potential financial benefits in exchange for wastewater service access, including a possible payment usable for debt service or to lower resident tax/utility rates. No dollar amount or finalized terms disclosed; City Council took no action.

Trade press reported Iron Mountain plan for a seven-building hyperscale Taylor Meadows campus on roughly 500 acres near Hutto — the company first Texas data center. First grid-connected buildings targeted for around 2030.

Community Impact reported the site was previously entitled for a residential subdivision of nearly 1,900 homes, and that the data center projected water use is lower than that build-out would have required.
Reporting noted that replacing the previously-approved ~1,900-home residential development with the data center campus is projected to reduce sanitary sewer/water demand.

projects.name: T5@ATL IV (Palmetto)
projects.note: New multi-building Atlanta-area campus scalable to 300MW with on-site substation, expected operational in 2026.

events.summary: T5 Data Centers filed a preliminary Development of Regional Impact (DRI) application with the Atlanta Regional Commission for a two-building, 495,000-sq-ft data center campus off I-85 and Gullatt Road near Fairburn, its third south-Atlanta-area campus at the time.
T5 withdrew its original DRI application, which by that point had grown to a proposed 2.95 million-sq-ft, 300MW campus across seven buildings.

T5 finalized acquisition of the 91-acre Palmetto/South Fulton County site and publicly announced the ATL IV campus, describing it as scalable up to 300MW with an on-site substation targeted for 2026 operation and liquid cooling to support AI workloads.

T5 submitted a revised, scaled-down DRI application for ATL IV consisting of three data center buildings totaling up to 1,320,000 sq ft along Gullatt Road, with supporting access roads, parking, utilities, and stormwater infrastructure.

The Atlanta Regional Commission completed its Development of Regional Impact review of the revised ATL IV application, a milestone reported as clearing the way toward construction; the Fairburn portion of the site already held full zoning/permits under existing industrial designation.
The City of Palmetto held a special city council session that advanced discussion of a potential economic development agreement tied to the T5 project.

The Palmetto City Council unanimously approved a rewritten industrial zoning code that permanently excludes data centers from the city, following community concern that had built up around the T5 project and area data-center growth; Mayor Teresa Thomas-Smith cited an "overall disinterest" in the warehouse-like structures.

projects.name: NTT VA11 Gainesville
projects.note: 96MW/300,000 sq ft facility (VA11) as first phase of a planned 336MW campus, due live early 2027; part of $10B+ NTT US buildout.

events.summary: Southview 66 LLC and Gainesville JM LC (with Lerner Enterprises) filed a rezoning and special-use-permit application for the I-66 and U.S. 29 Technology Park, a six-data-center plan on a 102-acre parcel — the site that later became NTT Grove at Gainesville campus.

Prince William County Board of Supervisors voted 6-2 to approve rezoning and a special-use permit for the I-66/U.S. 29 Technology Park, allowing six data centers outside the county Data Center Opportunity Zone overlay.

NTT Global Data Centers announced it had acquired 103 acres in Gainesville from Lerner Enterprises for $257.4 million to build a 336 MW, four-building, 2-million sq ft campus — its largest in the U.S.

Planning documents for NTT Grove at Gainesville campus became public, showing the project needs additional Army Corps of Engineers approval for wetlands impacts; filings hinted Amazon Web Services as the likely anchor tenant.
VA10, the first building on NTT Gainesville campus, became operational, delivering roughly 84 MW of critical IT load across about 295,680 sq ft of data floor space.

Dominion Energy held an informational meeting at Gainesville High School on its proposed Daves Store Substation and transmission line needed to power NTT and AWS Gainesville data centers, drawing resident pushback over visual impact.

Dominion Energy submitted its Daves Store transmission line/substation route to the Virginia State Corporation Commission for approval, part of ~1 GW of new power infrastructure needed to serve NTT and AWS Gainesville-area data centers.
Coalition to Protect Prince William County publicly criticized the Daves Store transmission line as an extension cord built to serve NTT and Amazon Gainesville data centers at ratepayer expense.

Prince William Times reported on the quarter-mile-long NTT data center building rising along I-66, noting community outrage, resident concerns about noise and electrical infrastructure, and removal of at least 40 acres of trees.

NTT DATA announced it secured nearly 115 MW in new capacity commitments across its Gainesville, Chicago, and Sacramento campuses as part of a $10 billion global data-center investment push through 2027; VA11 in Gainesville listed as available for pre-lease at 96 MW.

projects.name: DataBank Red Oak Campus
projects.note: 8-building campus (400MW substation, up to 300MW critical IT); first 3 buildings already leased, $2.0B construction financing secured April 2026.

events.summary: DataBank registered its first Red Oak building, DFW9 (425,170 sq ft, two-story data center with office space, $256M estimated cost), with the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation (TABS project TABS2024020821).

DataBank announced development of a 480MW, 292-acre, eight-building data center campus in Red Oak, Ellis County, Texas (its third new-campus announcement in 12 months), with Phase 1 covering four buildings and a 400MW Oncor substation delivering 240MW of critical IT power; initial ready-for-service targeted for Q2 2026.

DataBank filed plans for a second Red Oak building, DFW10 ($256M, 425,000+ sq ft), with construction slated to begin February 2025 and complete by mid-2028; report described it as a $256M addition to the growing Red Oak campus.

Dallas Express reported DataBank's $265M expansion of the Red Oak campus (second facility), a 425,000 sq ft two-story building designed by JHET Architects, with construction beginning February 2025 and completion expected July 2028; full build-out envisions eight buildings totaling 3.4M+ sq ft.
Construction work on DFW11 at the Red Oak campus began (per reported December 2025–January 2028 build schedule), part of the campus's staggered build-out following DFW9 and DFW10.

DataBank closed a $2.0 billion construction loan — its largest financing to date, led by MUFG Bank under DataBank's Green Financing Framework — to fund the first three Red Oak buildings (DFW9, DFW10, DFW11: 600,000 sq ft, 180MW), all fully leased to an AI/cloud tenant (reported to be Oracle); the financing was said to accelerate delivery by about 18 months.

Red Oak Planning & Zoning Commission and City Council held a separate, contentious public hearing on an unrelated 830-acre Compass Datacenters project elsewhere in Red Oak; over 150 residents attended amid a 1,600-signature opposition petition citing noise, water, traffic and power-grid concerns (noted here for context but distinct from DataBank's Stainback Road campus).

Reporting described DataBank's Red Oak campus in active construction, with initial concrete pours underway and electrical systems installation beginning; residents voiced mixed reactions including concerns about noise and water use, while DataBank held public meetings and appointed a community liaison.

DataBank closed $1.45 billion in new financing across two transactions: an $800M corporate revolving credit facility and a $650M upsize (including DataBank's first private-placement notes) of the Red Oak construction loan to fund a fourth building (60MW additional IT capacity), bringing total Red Oak campus financing to $2.65 billion.

Dallas Morning News reported DFW9 was expected to come online in August 2026, with DFW10 (interior work, ~$301M, completion January 2027) and DFW11 (~$315M, completion March 2027) following on a staggered schedule; residents cited concerns about scale, infrastructure strain, a 10-year tax-abatement delay on community benefits, and limited local job creation relative to project size.

Texas Governor Greg Abbott ordered a statewide audit of all data centers connecting to the ERCOT grid, effectively pausing new interconnections pending review — a state-level action affecting all Texas data center projects, including those on DataBank's Red Oak campus.

projects.name: CloudHQ Mount Prospect
projects.note: Village hired outside engineering firm to handle CloudHQ's permit reviews; also set up a dedicated public fact-check portal, signaling active community scrutiny.

events.summary: CloudHQ acquired the 49.7-acre former United Airlines world headquarters campus in Mount Prospect, Illinois.
Mount Prospect Village Board held a first reading of an ordinance granting a preliminary plat of subdivision and conditional use for CloudHQ proposed data center campus.
Daily Herald reported details of CloudHQ proposed $2.5 billion redevelopment of the former United Airlines headquarters site into a data center campus.
Mount Prospect Village Board held a first reading of an ordinance granting a conditional use for a final planned unit development and final plat for the three-building CloudHQ data center campus.

CloudHQ and ComEd broke ground on the $2.5 billion, 1.5 million-square-foot hyperscale data center campus on the former United Airlines site, with three buildings (each over 80MW) and a new ComEd substation.
ComEd and CloudHQ jointly announced the groundbreaking, citing a first-of-its-kind onsite substation, projected 1,000+ construction jobs per building, and first building completion targeted for 2024.

Mount Prospect Village Board approved an inducement resolution supporting CloudHQ application for a Cook County Class 6b property tax incentive, assessing the property at 10% of market value for the first 10 years.

Village Manager said the ComEd substation needed to power the CloudHQ site was expected complete by June; the village board also considered a $60,000 lobbying contract amid lingering state legislative hurdles.

Mount Prospect Village Board adopted an ordinance amending the conditional use, allowing CloudHQ to revise from three two-story buildings to two three-story buildings, a second substation, and mechanical yard; first building retargeted to 2027.
Mount Prospect trustees prepared to approve $3 million in CloudHQ developer contributions toward public improvements: multiuse path, street lighting, and Park District splash pad.
The Real Deal reported on CloudHQ $3 million community-benefits package tied to the Mount Prospect megaproject.
Mount Prospect hired outside firm HR Green at up to $22,500 to handle three CloudHQ permit reviews, citing roughly 3,700 sheets of construction drawings and 1,500+ pages of structural calculations.

projects.name: Vantage NV1 (Storey County)
projects.note: Vantage's entry into the Nevada market; 224MW campus, first two buildings fully leased, first building opening Q2 2026.

events.summary: Vantage Data Centers purchased approximately 137 acres near Electric Avenue and USA Parkway at the Tahoe-Reno Industrial Center in Storey County — the site that became the NV1 campus.

Vantage Data Centers NV11 LLC submitted a formal application to the Nevada Governor Office of Economic Development requesting sales/use and personal property tax abatements for the proposed Storey County data center.
Vantage broke ground on the NV1 campus at Tahoe-Reno Industrial Center, beginning construction of the NV11 and NV12 buildings.

Nevada Governor Office of Economic Development approved $19.2 million in tax abatements for Vantage, tied to a $254 million capital investment projected to generate $76 million in new tax revenue over 10 years while creating about 10 jobs.

Vantage publicly unveiled the NV1 campus: a nearly $3 billion, 224 MW, four-building, 1.1 million sq ft development on 137 acres in Storey County, with the first two buildings fully leased and the first building slated for Q2 2026.
Local press reported the $3 billion NV1 project pushing forward at TRIC, including comments from Storey County Manager Austin Osborne about managing hypergrowth from data center development.
Data Center Frontier profiled NV1 progress: over 805,000 labor hours logged, more than 700 workers on site daily, and a 0.25 Total Project Incident Rate on a 30-acre building pad.

McCarthy Building Companies held a topping-out ceremony for NV12, a 64 MW, 260,000 sq ft liquid-cooled building; the campus had surpassed 1.1 million labor hours with zero lost-time incidents, with NV12 phased turnover starting December 2027.

Nevada Current reported data centers water and power needs are straining Storey County, noting that Tahoe-Reno Industrial Center relies on groundwater basins with uncertain consumptive-use projections.

Carson Now reported an escalating legal battle over water availability at TRIC — where NV1 is sited — between TRIC developer and the quasi-governmental water/sewer provider, with trial set for spring 2027.

projects.name: Vantage VA4 Fredericksburg
projects.note: $2B, 192MW hyperscale campus (VA4); first building scheduled to open late 2027.

events.summary: After a marathon public hearing, the Stafford Board of Supervisors voted 4-2-1 to adopt a Comprehensive Plan update (R25-208) and zoning amendment (O25-29) imposing a 750-foot data-center setback from homes, schools and rivers (up from 100 feet); this date became the cutoff later used to grandfather VA4/Melrod under prior rules.

At the same hearing, residents including Falmouth's Alane Callander and groups like Friends of the Rappahannock pushed for setbacks as large as 1,500 feet and raised water, noise and viewshed concerns about the wave of Stafford data-center rezonings that includes Vantage's VA4/Melrod project.

Vantage Data Centers announced a $2 billion investment to build VA4, a 192MW, three-building, 929,000-sq-ft campus on 82 acres in Stafford County near Fredericksburg — its fourth Virginia campus, bringing statewide capacity to 782MW.

Vantage and general contractor DPR Construction held a groundbreaking ceremony for VA4, attended by Virginia Deputy Secretary of Commerce Luis Lopez Stipes, Stafford Supervisors Meg Bohmke and Darrell English, and IBEW Local 26; first building targeted for late 2027.

Stafford Board of Supervisors approved Ordinance O25-29(R), grandfathering five previously-approved data center projects — including Vantage VA-4 (Melrod) — allowing them to proceed under the pre-Oct. 21, 2025 zoning rules rather than the new setback/noise standards.
Environmental advocates and residents who fought for the October setback reforms objected to the grandfathering vote, arguing it undermined protections they had just won for projects like VA4/Melrod.

Virginia Business reported VA4 is expected to generate $115.4–$116.7 million in annual property tax revenue for Stafford County, while Protect Stafford president Erin Sanzero warned county officials were unprepared for the volume of data-center rezoning applications and that Stafford risked becoming 'the next Data Center Alley.'

Stafford Planning Commission voted 7-0 to recommend Board approval of a conditional use permit for a Vantage Data Centers VA41 LLC electric substation on 15.62 acres on Centerport Parkway (Hartwood District), to serve the VA4 campus's on-site power needs.
Stafford Board of Supervisors approved the conditional use permit for Vantage's on-site electric substation supporting the VA4 data center campus.

Potomac Local reported Stafford had five approved data-center projects (three, including VA4, under construction) and 11 pending applications amid a state budget fight; Virginia's compromise preserved data-center sales-tax equipment exemptions (~$2B/year statewide) while adding a new $0.011/kWh electricity consumption tax capped near $600M/year.

projects.name: Fort Meade Data Center Campus
projects.note: 4.4M sq ft hyperscale campus on former phosphate-mine land, $2.6-2.8B investment; city commissioners approved developer agreement April 14, 2026.

events.summary: Fort Meade City Commission voted 5-0 to approve land-use and zoning changes on roughly 1,164 acres to permit data center development, paired with a 10-year, $150 million tax incentive package.
About a dozen protesters gathered outside Fort Meade City Hall opposing the proposed Stonebridge/Bohler Places data center project.

Commissioners reclassified the development agreement from a resolution to an ordinance, requiring 10 days notice, first/second readings, and additional public hearings after Earthjustice raised procedural objections and ~20 residents opposed the project.
Fort Meade Planning and Zoning Board held a public hearing on the Stonebridge/Bohler Places development agreement.

Fort Meade Planning Commission voted unanimously to recommend the 20-year development agreement with Stonebridge; hearing covered 1.2 GW power needs, 100% backup generator capacity, and revised water-use figure of 50,000 gallons/day via closed-loop cooling.
Southwest Florida Water Management District adopted a new rule requiring a separate permit approval for the project water use.

Fort Meade City Commission unanimously approved a 20-year, $2.6-2.8 billion development agreement with Bohler Places LLC/Stonebridge for an 8-building, up to 4.4 million sq ft hyperscale data center campus on 1,300 acres of former phosphate mine; 40 of 41 public commenters opposed it.
Governor DeSantis administration publicly criticized Fort Meade handling of the project, citing concerns about utility rates and water use.

Florida Commerce Secretary J. Alex Kelly sent a letter calling the project fundamentally flawed, saying developer water estimates were woefully underestimated and flagging the lack of a disclosed end-user/operator.

Five Fort Meade residents filed two lawsuits seeking to void the city approval, alleging procedural violations, inadequate notice, and incompatibility with the comprehensive plan; trial projected for November 2027.
The Watchdogs of Fort Meade began circulating recall petitions against Mayor Jaret Williams, Vice Mayor Petrina McCutchen, and Commissioner Matthew Taylor over the data center approval.
Recall Committee Chairman Michael Bennett and supporters delivered recall petitions with over 1,000 signatures to Fort Meade City Hall, to be verified by the Polk County Supervisor of Elections.

projects.name: Atlas Capital Bloomfield
projects.note: Proposed 1M-sq-ft data center at 132 Griffin Road North; surfaced at a June 26, 2026 Town Plan and Zoning Commission meeting.

events.summary: Atlas Capital Group gave an informal, conceptual presentation to the Bloomfield Town Plan and Zoning Commission about a potential 1-million-square-foot data center at 132 Griffin Road North.
Data Center Dynamics reported that Atlas Capital Group, a New York/LA real estate investment firm, may develop a roughly 1 million-square-foot data center in Bloomfield, Connecticut.
Atlas Capital representative said the project planned 127,000-square-foot open-air substation is required for a facility of this size and that the company has had preliminary talks with Eversource.
Stamford Advocate reported on the New York developer proposal for a massive data center in Bloomfield, covering the 44-acre former tobacco-field site and project scope.

Sentry Commercial reported conceptual plans for a roughly 1 million-square-foot data center in Hartford County, detailing the 900,000-square-foot data hall and 127,000-square-foot substation on a 44-acre parcel.
The Town of Bloomfield issued a public news release announcing Atlas Capital Group conceptual data center proposal for the Griffin Road North site.

projects.name: NE Edge Millstone (Waterford)
projects.note: 1.5M-sq-ft data center proposed to draw power directly from Millstone nuclear plant; host-fee agreement lapsed after nearly 3 years of local opposition, effectively ending the project.

events.summary: NE Edge, managed by George A. McLaughlin III, publicly proposed a 1.5M-sq-ft, ~300MW data center on Dominion Energy's Millstone Power Station property in Waterford, CT, drawing power directly from the nuclear plant.
NE Edge detailed plans for a two-building data center at Millstone, committing to pay Waterford $231 million over 30 years in lieu of property taxes.
Waterford's Representative Town Meeting and First Selectman Rob Brule unanimously approved the host fee agreement with NE Edge, which included guidelines on sound and environmental impact.

NE Edge-Waterford, LLC and the Town of Waterford signed a Data Center Host Municipality Fee Agreement committing NE Edge to pay $231M in lieu-of-tax fees over 30 years, with a clause requiring building permits by March 2026.
NE Edge purchased a parcel of land in Connecticut connected to the Millstone-area data center development.

Dominion Energy Nuclear Connecticut filed Petition No. 1586 with the CT Siting Council seeking a declaratory ruling that no new Certificate of Environmental Compatibility was required to revise the Millstone site boundary to lease parcels to NE Edge.
The Connecticut Siting Council declined to issue Dominion's requested declaratory ruling on the Millstone site boundary revision, finding it premature — a key setback for the NE Edge project.

Shoreline residents raised concerns at a town meeting about noise, property values, electric rates, and wildlife impacts; opposition group Concerned Citizens of Waterford and East Lyme (CCWEL), with over 50 members, was active in opposing the site.
CT Mirror reported on the Millstone-powered data center proposal, detailing the project's direct power arrangement with Dominion and mounting community and regulatory scrutiny.
CT legislature's Energy and Technology Committee voted 12-3 to advance a bill requiring ISO New England and local utilities to study grid impact of the NE Edge behind-the-meter data center.
Waterford opponents petitioned the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission to intervene and block the NE Edge proposal, citing concerns tied to proximity to the Millstone nuclear plant.
Coverage described NE Edge as a hyperscale facility for AI training driven by ~300MW of power (about 15% of Millstone's output), unprecedented in scale for Connecticut.
Waterford's Board of Selectmen voted 2-1 to permit NE Edge, LLC to assign its host fee agreement to a subsidiary company, NE Edge-Waterford, LLC.
U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal teamed up with a Republican senator on federal legislation to rein in data centers, amid continued Connecticut concern over projects like the Waterford proposal.

The deadline for NE Edge to obtain building permits passed without the company meeting it; Waterford First Selectman Rob Brule announced the host fee agreement had ended, effectively killing the project after nearly three years of local opposition.
CT Mirror published a review of the full arc of the NE Edge fight, characterizing it as a defeated Connecticut data center project after sustained community and regulatory resistance.

projects.name: Quantica Big Sky Campus
projects.note: 5,000-acre campus; NorthWestern Energy committed up to 1,000 MW to Quantica as of July 2026, with Phase I construction slated for 2026.

events.summary: Invenergy requested interconnection to NorthWestern Energy's Broadview substation, the earliest step in what would become the Big Sky Campus site's grid access.
Broad Reach Power purchased the Broadview interconnection project from Invenergy, with Daniel Zolnikov serving as local developer.
ENGIE acquired Broad Reach Power, folding the Broadview-area power project into its portfolio ahead of the Quantica spinout.
Montana Property LLC quietly acquired roughly 5,000 acres (about eight square miles) south of Broadview, later revealed as the land assembly for Quantica's Big Sky Campus.
NorthWestern Energy announced a $25-30 million transmission line project tied to the Broadview substation area, with expected completion in 2028.

NorthWestern Energy signed a letter of intent to serve Quantica Infrastructure's Montana data center development, committing to a Phase 1 load of 500 MW growing to 1 GW, with initial service possible as early as 2026.
Montana's Energy and Technology Interim Committee met to study the state's power generation capacity amid data-center growth, launching studies due by September 2026.

Montana Public Radio/MEIC reported NorthWestern's proposed 1,000 MW commitment is roughly equivalent to the power used to serve 800,000 homes, more than all of NorthWestern's residential customers combined.
Quantica Infrastructure introduced Big Sky Digital Infrastructure (BSDI) as its flagship Montana development platform for the 5,000-acre Big Sky Campus, with construction planned to begin in 2026.
The Montana Public Service Commission decided to keep NorthWestern Energy's letters of intent with three data-center developers confidential as trade secrets.
The Butte-Silver Bow Council of Commissioners sent a letter to the PSC advocating separate rate classifications to shield existing ratepayers from data-center-driven boom-bust risk.

AP/Montana Free Press reported Quantica does not yet hold water rights for the Broadview site and is evaluating zero-water air cooling, deep aquifer wells, treated greywater, and direct-to-chip liquid cooling.

A coalition including Earthjustice, MEIC, NW Energy Coalition, and Honor the Earth sent a letter to the Montana PSC demanding disclosure of NorthWestern's talks with 11 additional data-center developers.

Daily Montanan reported NorthWestern Energy was in talks with at least 11 additional data-center entities beyond Atlas, Sabey, and Quantica, which combined could draw enough power for 1.6 million homes.
Quantica's July 2025 letter of intent with NorthWestern progressed into a signed development agreement by roughly the first quarter of 2026.
Broadview-area residents divided; resident Cari Olson founded Just One Montanan to push for a three-year statewide construction moratorium on data centers pending legislative action.
Earthjustice filed a motion before the Montana PSC on behalf of seven groups challenging the December 2025 decision keeping NorthWestern's data-center letters of intent confidential.
Quantica filed interconnection applications with NorthWestern Energy seeking to expand generation capacity at the Big Sky Campus roughly seven-fold, from about 1,000 MW to 7,235 MW.
Broadview resident Kassi Solberg submitted a citizen ballot initiative petition to Yellowstone County requiring two-thirds voter approval before any data center could be built or expanded.
Quantica signed an agreement with a Montana union federation covering the Big Sky Campus project, though coverage criticized it for being thin on enforceable labor details.
The Yellowstone County attorney's office approved the ballot language for the citizen data-center initiative, allowing signature gathering to proceed toward the November ballot.
Daily Montanan reported on a growing citizen movement across Montana counties seeking direct voter oversight of data-center construction.
Yellowstone County commissioners held a meeting at which details of a planned lawsuit challenging the legality of the citizen data-center ballot initiative were distributed.

Yellowstone County asserted this date was the actual legal deadline for signature collection on the data-center ballot initiative, after officials said they learned of a 2025 election-statute change following contact from Quantica's attorney.
Yellowstone County commissioners proposed a new policy restricting signature-gathering for citizen initiatives, amid the ongoing dispute over the data-center ballot measure.
Yellowstone County commissioners announced the true signature-gathering deadline had already passed on July 13, effectively blocking the initiative from the November ballot.

A Yellowstone County District Court judge ruled the signature-collection deadline had passed, keeping the two-thirds-voter-approval data-center initiative off the November ballot despite over 12,000 of the required 16,650 signatures collected.

projects.name: Applied Digital Deuel County (withdrawn)
projects.note: $5B, 430MW campus near Toronto, SD; withdrawn after 2026 legislature rejected a sales-tax exemption for data centers.

events.summary: Applied Digital proposed a ~$5B, 430MW AI data center campus (two ~907,500 sq ft buildings) on a 150-200 acre site east of Toronto in Deuel County, South Dakota, with total project impact estimated at $10-16 billion.

South Dakota Searchlight reported the clock was ticking on a data center tax incentive proposal as the legislative session and elections loomed, with Applied Digital's Deuel County project tied to the outcome.
The South Dakota House State Affairs Committee voted 9-3 to kill House Bill 1005, which would have granted a 50-year sales tax exemption on data center equipment and software purchases.

Senate committees advanced competing data center bills: SB 135 (requiring data centers to pay their own costs, 5-4) and SB 239 (a narrower 30-year tax exemption, 6-3); Applied Digital VP said losing the exemption would cost roughly $2B more to build in South Dakota.
A data center regulation bill passed the South Dakota House as the legislature moved toward restrictions rather than incentives.
Governor Larry Rhoden signed SB 135 and related bills into law, requiring data centers to cover their own electricity rate impacts and water-use costs and protecting local ordinances.

Applied Digital VP Nick Phillips said the $5B Deuel County project 'doesn't make sense at this time' after the legislature's rejection of tax incentives, confirming the company would let its land agreement near Toronto lapse.
New state laws took effect including data center regulatory measures (electricity cost pass-through bans, water-use disclosure, local ordinance protection) enacted after the incentive bills failed.

projects.name: Gemini Sioux Falls Technology Park
projects.note: 500MW hyperscale campus on 164 acres next to Xcel's Split Rock Substation; received unanimous rezoning approval from Sioux Falls City Council on January 6, 2026.

events.summary: Gemini Data Center SD LLC acquired roughly 164 acres from Xcel Energy adjacent to Xcel Split Rock Substation in northeast Sioux Falls, laying groundwork for the proposed 500 MW Sioux Falls Technology Park.
Sioux Falls City Council approved reclassifying the property from Tier III to Tier I growth-priority area, an unusual leapfrogging of the normal phased growth sequence.

SDPB reported LA-based Gemini Capital through Gemini Data Center SD LLC is seeking to build a hyperscale data center on land bought from Xcel Energy; project representative Kyle Peters confirmed an internal 500 MW capacity target contingent on state tax incentives.

City Council voted 7-0 to annex approximately 164 acres east of Veterans Parkway for the Gemini project; city filed a notice of claim making Gemini responsible for future infrastructure costs if it walks away.

City Council held a nearly six-hour public hearing on the rezoning with overflow attendance; more than 50 speakers, mostly opposed, raised concerns about energy consumption, water use, electronic waste, and lack of community benefit.

Council voted 7-0 to rezone roughly 145.6 acres from agricultural to light industrial with conditions: 200-ft setback, ~17 acres conservation, closed-loop cooling, domestic-only water use, city noise standards.
Following the rezoning vote, opponents shouted expletives and criticism at the dais, prompting a five-minute recess; local coverage captured the outrage.
Grassroots group Let Sioux Falls Vote launched a petition drive seeking to force a citywide referendum on the rezoning, needing 6,704 valid signatures by January 29.

Reporting confirmed Gemini completed its interconnection application and system impact study with Xcel Energy and is funding a facility study; a formal power agreement (subject to PUC review) still to be negotiated.
Let Sioux Falls Vote submitted 378 petition sheets to the city clerk after more than 100 volunteers canvassed for 20 days in sub-zero temperatures.
City announced the referendum petition contained only 5,012 valid signatures, about 1,700 short of the 6,704 required; the petition was rejected and the rezoning remained in effect.

SD House State Affairs Committee voted 9-3 to kill HB 1005, which would have granted data centers a 50-year sales-and-use tax exemption; an amendment offering a tiered 10-35 year exemption also failed.

SD Senate committee advanced SB 135, the Data Center Bill of Rights for Citizens, requiring large data centers to cover costs tied to meeting their power demands including exit costs if a project falls through.

A1 Development Solutions (Gemini local consulting firm) sued its own project representative Kyle Peters (Gov. Noem son-in-law) alleging he covertly diverted the data-center client and others while still under contract.
SD Senate passed SB 135 34-0 after striking language that would have banned state/local tax exemptions for data centers.
Gemini launched a public website for the Sioux Falls Technology Park describing Gemini Family Office role in land ownership, planning, permitting, and coordination.
SD House passed SB 135 60-7 with amendment applying the law to data centers with 10 MW or greater peak electrical use, requiring those projects to cover power-demand costs.

Governor signed SB 135, the Data Center Bill of Rights, into law — statewide cost-protection rules for large data center power demands (10 MW+) applicable to the Gemini project eventual Xcel service agreement.

projects.name: Microsoft Cheyenne Expansion
projects.note: Microsoft announced intent to acquire ~3,200 acres in southeast Cheyenne for a multiyear data-center expansion, building on its Black Hills Energy partnership.

events.summary: Wyoming Gov. Dave Freudenthal signed HB 67, exempting data centers that buy or rent more than $2 million in computing equipment annually from state sales tax.
Microsoft established its first data center presence in Cheyenne, Wyoming.
Microsoft expanded its original Cheyenne data center footprint, adding capacity to its existing campus.
Microsoft opened two additional data centers in Cheyenne, further building out its Wyoming campus.
The Wyoming Legislature extended the state data-center sales-and-use tax exemption through 2042.
Microsoft, with JE Dunn as general contractor, began heavy earthwork on a new data center campus on HR Ranch Road east of Cheyenne, with completion targeted for early 2026.

Microsoft announced intent to purchase roughly 3,200 acres in Cheyenne to roughly triple its data center footprint, pledging over $68 million in off-site infrastructure improvements and no reliance on local property tax incentives.

Microsoft detailed a utility partnership with Black Hills Energy under the Large Power Contract Service (LPCS) tariff, under which Microsoft funds the full cost of electricity infrastructure so other ratepayers are not burdened.
Microsoft said it would minimize water use and fund replenishment projects in Cheyenne, with partners including Trout Unlimited, expected to restore an estimated 566 million gallons of water.
Opposition to Cheyenne data center growth intensified as the city moved to accommodate further development, with residents raising sustained objections.
Angry Cheyenne residents spoke out at a public meeting against the proposed annexation and Microsoft data center project.
A Wyoming state legislator said the state needs to determine how revenue from the data center boom should be distributed among local governments and residents.
Wyoming residents pressed for clarity on where water for the expanding data center boom would come from in the semi-arid region.
The Cheyenne City Council rejected a proposed 12-month moratorium on new data center development by an 8-1 vote after hours of debate over water, noise, and long-term community impacts.
Wyoming Public Media reported on the city council rejection of a data center moratorium, noting no pause on development despite resident concerns.
The Cheyenne Planning Commission held a five-hour hearing on Microsoft 3,200-acre southside expansion, recommending denial for most components.

Microsoft data center annexation/zoning plans failed to secure the Cheyenne Planning Commission endorsement, with two parcels near Laramie County Community College falling short of the required votes.
Coverage explained Wyoming data center sales tax exemption, worth up to $22.6 million annually, and its extension through 2042.
The Cheyenne City Council rejected a proposal to slow down the Microsoft land annexation process, clearing the way for a final vote.

After a seven-hour public hearing with overwhelming resident opposition, the Cheyenne City Council passed Ordinance 4687 by a 6-3 vote, annexing roughly 3,460 acres into the city for Microsoft planned data center campus.
Reporting confirmed Cheyenne grew by 3,500 acres after the controversial Microsoft-related annexation vote following more than five hours of council discussion.
Opponents launched a referendum petition drive seeking to reverse the Cheyenne City Council 3,460-acre annexation vote, needing roughly 2,700 signatures within 20 days.

Referendum organizers submitted 3,275-plus signatures seeking a public vote to reverse the Microsoft annexation, exceeding the roughly 2,739 registered-voter threshold required to force a November ballot measure.

projects.name: STAK Energy North Slope Campus
projects.note: $500M, up to 3GW natural-gas-powered AI data center campus on 715 leased acres ~26 mi south of Deadhorse; received preliminary state land-lease approval, construction targeted summer 2026.

events.summary: Stak Energy submitted its initial application to Alaska DNR Division of Oil and Gas for a 50-year state land lease (ADL 422741) covering 715.4 acres off the Dalton Highway near Milepost 390 for a natural-gas-powered AI data center campus; DNR solicited competing bids and none came in.
Stak Energy filed a revised application amending its original lease submission to the Division of Oil and Gas.
Alaska DNR issued a preliminary best-interest finding for the proposed 50-year land lease to Stak Energy, granting preliminary approval for the 715-acre parcel.
Alaska Beacon broke the story of the proposed $500 million, up-to-3GW natural-gas-powered Stak Energy data center campus on the North Slope.
Anchorage Daily News expanded coverage detailing the 715-acre footprint, dry-air cooling advantage, and lack of a firm natural-gas supply deal at time of filing.
Alaska Public Media reported on the proposal, noting Stak Energy Alaska roots and staffing plans.

Northern Alaska Environmental Center published an analysis of the lease documents identifying unresolved risks: incomplete wetland delineation, no permafrost thermal modeling, no bird/caribou surveys, undisclosed lease financial terms, and estimated gas consumption of 128-183 billion cubic feet per year.

The Alaska Center publicized environmental concerns including potential heat-island warming effects extending up to 6.2 miles, the need for 7 million cubic yards of gravel to raise the site 5-7 feet, and fuel consumption potentially exceeding twice urban Alaska electrical generation; urged residents to file public comments.
Original public comment deadline on the DNR preliminary best-interest decision for the Stak Energy lease.
Coverage reported Alaskans had flooded the state comment docket with opposition, including submissions reading "HELL NO! To ANY DATA CENTERS" and "NO AI," ahead of the extended comment deadline.

Anchorage Daily News reported more than 500 public comments submitted to DNR, with fewer than a dozen supporting the project and the vast majority opposed; Stak Energy characterized most as form letters.
Extended deadline (4:30 p.m.) for public comments on the proposed 50-year land lease; DNR said it would assess comments before issuing a final lease decision.

projects.name: Imperial Valley Data Center
projects.note: ~950,000-1M sq ft AI/ML data center; county supervisors approved it in April 2026 then reversed course, imposing a 45-day moratorium after water-use and air-quality opposition; developer sued over the moratorium.

events.summary: Developer Sebastian Rucci registers Imperial Valley Computer Manufacturing, LLC and related entities in California to pursue the Imperial County AI/ML data center project.

Imperial County Planning & Development Services distributes a formal 'Request for Review and Comments' to stakeholders, opening the official agency review process for the ~950,000-1M sq ft, 330MW data center.

Imperial County treats the project as exempt from CEQA review (citing a 2024 state 'advanced manufacturing' exemption for industrially-zoned land) and files a CEQA exemption for the grading permit, allowing preliminary site work.
The City of Imperial withdraws from a recycled-wastewater supply agreement with the developer, undercutting IVCM's plan to avoid using potable/Colorado River water.
The City of El Centro also backs out of a proposed recycled-water arrangement for the project.
The City of Imperial files a CEQA lawsuit challenging Imperial County's decision to treat the data center (including its battery backup system) as exempt from environmental review.

State Senator Steve Padilla sends a letter to the Imperial County Board of Supervisors calling for full public environmental review of the project, questioning the CEQA exemption given the facility's scale and water/energy demands.

IVCM files a federal civil rights lawsuit against the City of Imperial and named officials, alleging a coordinated campaign of administrative obstruction and retaliation intended to derail the $10B project.

KPBS reports over 2,000 residents have signed a petition opposing the project over water scarcity and grid-strain concerns, and that a lot-merger vote before the Board of Supervisors remains the final approval step.

The Imperial County Board of Supervisors votes 4-1 to approve a lot merger clearing the way for the nearly 1-million-sq-ft data center, during a contentious hearing marked by restricted public access and at least one arrest.
IVCM formally applies to the Imperial Irrigation District (IID) for 880 acre-feet of water annually to supply the project.
IID denies IVCM's water request, citing Regulation 21's 300-foot restriction near municipal water supplies.
Imperial County supervisors hold a public hearing to consider a moratorium on new data center approvals amid mounting opposition.

After reclaimed-wastewater negotiations collapse, IVCM sues the Imperial Irrigation District in Imperial County Superior Court on eight legal claims, seeking roughly 260 million gallons of Colorado River water annually — reversing its earlier pledge to avoid Colorado River water.

The Imperial County Board of Supervisors unanimously approves an urgency interim ordinance imposing a 45-day moratorium on approvals/permits for new or pending data center facilities in unincorporated areas, and creates a Data Center Advisory Committee.
IVCM sues Imperial County in Superior Court challenging the moratorium, arguing the county used a 'manufactured emergency' pretext to reverse its April approval under public pressure.
The Board of Supervisors unanimously votes to extend the data center moratorium by 10 months and 15 days, blocking new permits until June 2027 while the advisory committee rewrites zoning rules.
Judge Jeffrey Jones hears IVCM's challenge to the county's data center moratorium in Imperial County Superior Court; a ruling is pending.
Judge Anderholt hears arguments in the CEQA case over whether the project requires a full environmental review; a ruling is expected within 90 days.

projects.name: Goodman Innovation Centre San Jose
projects.note: Two-building, 414,000 sq ft data center campus (97MW) on 45.8-acre infill site bought for $200M; expected operational 2028.

events.summary: City of San Jose released an Initial Study/Mitigated Negative Declaration for the 350 West Trimble Road Project, covering a rezoning and Planned Development Permit for a 208,000 sq ft manufacturing and assembly building on the 10.9-acre parcel.
San Jose Planning Commission approved LBA Realty industrial project at 350 West Trimble Road: a 208,000 sq ft manufacturing/assembly building with 15 loading docks, removing 57 trees.
A Goodman Group affiliate bought the 45.8-acre site at 350 and 370 West Trimble Road from an LBA Realty affiliate in an all-cash $200 million deal.

Goodman Group announced plans to redevelop the acquired Trimble Road site into the Goodman Innovation Centre San Jose, a two-building data center campus totaling roughly 414,000 sq ft with up to 97.3 MW of power available by 2028.

KQED reported that a proposed data center on West Trimble Road in San Jose would remove 224 trees to build a facility with 21 backup generators and a private electrical substation, cited amid broader resident concerns over water, power-grid strain, and health impacts.

projects.name: Valar Atomics Orangeville SMR
projects.note: Nearly-waterless 30MW AI data center powered by Valar's Ward250 small modular reactor with Nvidia's direct liquid cooling.

events.summary: Valar Atomics emerged from stealth with a $19 million seed round led by Riot Ventures and announced plans to build small modular nuclear reactors, initially with a pilot site agreement in the Philippines.

U.S. Department of Energy issued a Request for Application for its Reactor Pilot Program, an expedited authorization pathway for advanced test reactors with a goal of at least three reactors reaching criticality by July 4, 2026.
Emery County Commission hosted a town hall where Valar Atomics representatives answered citizen questions and safety concerns about the proposed Ward 250 test reactor at the San Rafael Energy Lab.
DOE announced Valar Atomics as one of 10 companies selected for its Reactor Pilot Program, authorizing construction and testing of the Ward 250 reactor at Utah San Rafael Energy Lab in Orangeville.
Valar Atomics and the Utah San Rafael Energy Lab broke ground on the Ward 250 test reactor site in Orangeville, Emery County.
Valar Atomics raised $130 million in Series A funding led by Snowpoint, Day One, and Dream Ventures, bringing total funding to over $150 million.
Valar Atomics received preliminary Documented Safety Analysis (DSA) approval under the DOE Reactor Pilot Program for the Ward 250 test reactor.

The Ward 250 reactor core was transported via three U.S. Air Force C-17 aircraft from March Air Reserve Base to Hill Air Force Base, then trucked to the Utah San Rafael Energy Lab, targeting operation by July 4, 2026.
Emery County Commission approved a letter of support for Valar Atomics as the Ward 250 reactor arrived in the Castle Country region, citing job and tax base benefits.
Valar Atomics received final Documented Safety Analysis (DSA) approval, clearing the way for power ascension testing of the Ward 250 reactor.

Valar Atomics Ward 250 high-temperature gas reactor achieved zero-power criticality at the San Rafael Energy Lab, becoming the second reactor to go critical under the DOE Reactor Pilot Program and the first DOE-authorized reactor built entirely outside a national laboratory.

Valar Atomics and Nvidia announced a partnership to explore a 30-megawatt, nearly waterless AI data center in Orangeville powered by roughly six Ward-class reactors, using Nvidia DSX liquid-cooling technology; the Ward 250 also powered an Nvidia DGX Spark AI chip, a first for U.S. nuclear power.

Valar Atomics raised a $1 billion Series B round led by Sequoia Capital (plus a $200 million credit facility), tripling its valuation to $6 billion, to fund mass production of factory-built nuclear reactors for AI data centers.

projects.name: Drox Group Rural Hall
projects.note: 129-acre hyperscale campus; Planning Board recommended denying rezoning despite developer concessions ($80M projected tax revenue over 10 years).

events.summary: The Drox Group filed a rezoning application (case F-1669) to rezone a 129-acre parcel near Rural Hall from agricultural to Heavy Industrial for a data center campus.
A community petition opposing the Rural Hall data center rezoning grew to more than 2,100 signatures.
Rural Hall Town Council adopted Resolution 901, formally opposing the proposed data center rezoning.
The Winston-Salem/Forsyth County Planning Board voted 7-2 to recommend denial of the rezoning application.
Drox Group representative offered concessions including capping noise below 60 dB and cited nearly $80 million in projected tax revenue over 10 years.
Rural Hall Town Council reversed course, adopting Resolution 912 withdrawing its opposition; meeting was announced only three days prior and residents were not allowed to speak.
A community forum on the proposed data center drew a large turnout of concerned residents.
A panel discussion on the Rural Hall data center proposal was hosted by community groups.
Local public radio reported the Rural Hall data center rezoning case was headed to a public hearing before county commissioners, with over 400 public emails submitted.
The Forsyth County Board of Commissioners voted 5-2 to deny the rezoning application for the Drox Group data center.

projects.name: Mountain Road Technology Park
projects.note: 427-acre, five-building campus; up to 2M gal/day water peak. Planning Commission approved 6-1 (Apr 16) but Board of Supervisors denied rezoning, height exception, and substation permit 4-3 (May 27, 2026).

events.summary: Hanover County Planning Commission approved the rezoning 6-1.
Board of Supervisors denied rezoning, height exception, and substation permit 4-3.

projects.name: Project Spero
projects.note: $3B facility seeking 450 MW (Phase 1 up to 100 MW) at Tyger River Industrial Park-North. Residents filed lawsuit demanding public planning review (Jul 8); SC PSC held oral arguments Aug 5 over whether project needs state-level review — largest PSC turnout since 2018.

events.summary: TigerDC / NorthMark Strategies / Valara Holdings announced $3B, 450 MW data center at Tyger River Industrial Park-North.
Residents filed lawsuit demanding public planning review of the project.
SC Public Service Commission held oral arguments over whether the project needs state-level review; largest PSC hearing turnout since 2018.

projects.name: Saxum Investment Data Center
projects.note: 230-acre rezoning request (agricultural/residential to heavy industrial) on Forest Ave in northwest Jackson. Hearing postponed May 27 after community pushback; City Council paused all DC construction June 23 pending new regulations.

events.summary: Rezoning hearing postponed after organized community pushback.
Jackson City Council paused all data center construction pending new regulations.

projects.name: Google Hermantown Campus
projects.note: 26 parcels / 278 acres in SW Hermantown. Community pushback forced a redo of the environmental review; second public comment period on draft AUAR + mitigation plan opened June 12, 2026 (closed Jul 16).

events.summary: Initial Alternative Urban Areawide Review (AUAR) adopted.
Second public comment period opened on revised Draft AUAR and Mitigation Plan after community pushback forced a redo of the environmental review. Comment period closed July 16.

projects.name: 100 Jersey Avenue AI Data Center
projects.note: 27,000 sq ft DC at 100 Jersey Avenue; City Council killed the proposal Feb 18, 2026 to audience applause. Hundreds held 'No data center!' signs; NAACP president cited neighborhood concerns. Site will become 600 apartments + park instead.

events.summary: City Council voted to cancel the data center. Hundreds attended with 'No data center!' signs. NAACP president Bruce Morgan cited neighborhood opposition. Site to be redeveloped as 600 apartments, warehouses, and a public park.

projects.name: Paducah Data Center Campus
projects.note: 1.8 GW campus on former DOE Paducah uranium-enrichment site; $100B+ private investment, 2 GW gas plant + 2.6 GW battery. NextEra building energy infra. ~600 permanent / 8,000 construction jobs. KY PSC approval pending. Completion target 2031.

events.summary: DOE announced Brookfield selected to develop 1.8 GW data center campus on the former Paducah Gaseous Diffusion Plant site; NextEra Energy building 2 GW gas plant + 2.6 GW battery storage. $100B+ private investment.

projects.name: QTS Van Wert Campus
projects.note: ~$10B capital investment in northwest Ohio; first building operational ~2029, full buildout ~2032.

events.summary: City of Van Wert and QTS announced data center campus in northwest Ohio; ~$10B capital investment, first building ~2029, full buildout ~2032.

projects.name: Southeast Raleigh Data Center
projects.note: Proposal pulled from City Council agenda in August 2026 after organized public opposition before it reached a vote.

events.summary: Developer pulled the proposal from the Raleigh City Council agenda after organized public opposition.

projects.name: Tulare County Data Center (moratorium)
projects.note: County Supervisors passed a 45-day moratorium on new data centers in August 2026, pausing all pending applications countywide.

events.summary: Tulare County Board of Supervisors passed 45-day moratorium on new data center applications.

projects.name: Meta-BlackRock El Paso Data Center
projects.note: $10B+ Meta-BlackRock strategic venture; 4,000 peak construction jobs, capacity beginning 2028.

events.summary: Meta announced $10B+ strategic venture with BlackRock to develop data center in El Paso; 4,000 peak construction jobs, capacity beginning 2028.

projects.name: La Osa
projects.note: Originally 59 data centers + 2 gas plants on 3,300 acres; scaled back 80% to 11 data centers (1 GW) after ~60 verbal comments and 50 emails all opposing.

events.summary: Board heard rezoning; ~60 verbal comments and 50 emails all opposed.

projects.name: Midtown Data Center
projects.note: 120 MW / $3B campus near the Armory; CUP upheld with conditions (no diesel testing on bad air days, on-site renewables) after 11-hour hearing.

events.summary: Board of Adjustment unanimously upheld CUP with air-quality and renewables conditions.

projects.name: I-20/Liberty Road Data Center
projects.note: 4.4M sq ft / 700+ acres; commissioners voted 4-1 to deny after noise demonstrations and 11 existing DCs cited.

events.summary: Commission voted 4-1 to deny rezoning. Residents presented noise demos.

projects.name: Inver Grove Heights Data Center
projects.note: 55,000 sq ft / 5 MW; 1-year moratorium passed 3-2 after 700+ petition signatures. Developer threatening $150M+ lawsuit.

events.summary: Council voted 3-2 for 1-year moratorium. Developer threatened $150M+ suit.

projects.name: Dulles Cloud South
projects.note: ~2,000-acre / 43M sq ft rezoning rejected days after Digital Gateway collapsed.

events.summary: Board rejected rezoning days after Digital Gateway legal fight ended.

projects.name: Project Tango
projects.note: Commissioners voted 5-1 to deny after 12+ hours of testimony on noise, water, traffic.

events.summary: Palm Beach County commissioners voted 5-1 to deny after 12+ hours of testimony.

projects.name: Project Marvel
projects.note: $14B, 700-acre campus; rezoning delayed amid opposition from residents and county officials.

events.summary: NDA covering Project Marvel becomes effective, signed by Bessemer mayor, city attorney, and chief of staff (expires February 2027); its existence only became public in July 2026.
Project Marvel first reported: a 4.5M-sq-ft, ~700-acre, 18-building hyperscale data center campus proposed for Bessemer by Logistics Land Investment LLC (affiliate of Atlanta TPA Group).
Bessemer Planning and Zoning Commission votes unanimously to add data centers as a permitted zoning use, clearing a procedural path for the project.

Neighboring residents file suit against the City of Bessemer seeking a TRO, alleging inadequate public notice, NDA-driven lack of transparency, and threats to watercress darter/bald eagle habitat and Little Blue/Five Mile creeks.
Bessemer City Council pulls the Project Marvel zoning request from its meeting agenda without discussion or a vote, pausing the proposal amid the new lawsuit.
Judge David Hobdy grants a temporary restraining order halting the city rezoning process (valid for 10 days).
Judge Hobdy dissolves the TRO, allowing Bessemer to restart the project through planning and zoning; outstanding motions continued to August hearing.
Alabama Reflector reports Bessemer residents demanding answers about the proposed 4-million-square-foot data center and the secrecy surrounding it.
Inside Climate News details the threatened watercress darter fish habitat that could be affected by the data center construction and water use.
Inside Climate News reports Bessemer could face further legal action over the project environmental impacts.
Inside Climate News publishes a fact-check of competing claims (water use, jobs, tax revenue) about the proposed hyperscale data center.
Alabama Reflector examines how the proposed hyperscale data center could affect Bessemer, covering water, power, and noise concerns.
Court hearing before Judge Hobdy on the city motion to dismiss and plaintiffs motion for expedited discovery in the rezoning lawsuit.
Alabama Reflector reports the project hits a speed bump amid continued community opposition.
Alabama Reflector reports new obstacles: a conflict with the planned Northern Beltline highway route and continued endangered-fish concerns.

Bessemer City Council votes 5-2 to adopt the rezoning ordinance converting roughly 700 acres from A-1 Agricultural to I-1 Light Industrial, approving Project Marvel over transparency and environmental objections.
Alabama Reflector and Southern Environmental Law Center report on the council approval of the rezoning despite unresolved environmental concerns.
Judge Hobdy orders plaintiffs to amend their complaint within 14 days and schedules a final hearing for March 19, 2026.
WBRC reports the ongoing lawsuit could force the city to disclose documents council members reviewed before the rezoning vote.
Developer announces it will request rezoning of an additional roughly 900 acres, expanding the campus footprint and shifting it away from the Northern Beltline corridor.
City of Bessemer announces the developer is acquiring additional land to create larger residential buffer zones around the expanded campus plan.
Bessemer City Council sets a public hearing to amend the city industrial zoning ordinance for the Project Marvel expansion.

Bessemer Planning and Zoning Commission votes 6-1 to recommend rezoning an additional 914 acres for light-industrial use, bringing the total campus to roughly 1,600 acres and 18 buildings (1.2GW capacity).
Public hearing held on amending the city industrial zoning ordinance for the expanded Project Marvel footprint.
Final scheduled hearing before Judge Hobdy in the original rezoning lawsuit.

After a public hearing where dozens of residents spoke (one called the project "an invasion"), Bessemer City Council votes 5-2 to approve rezoning of roughly 900-914 additional acres for the expanded Project Marvel campus.
Jefferson County Circuit Court Judge Hobdy grants a joint stipulation of dismissal, ending the original rezoning lawsuit with prejudice.
QTS Data Centers (owned by Blackstone) confirms it is the developer behind Project Marvel, after an affiliate purchased the property in land deals worth more than $870 million.

Southern Environmental Law Center and Alabama Rivers Alliance publicly question the Project Marvel NDA after obtaining it via Open Records Act; NDA required officials to destroy communications with the developer.
WBRC reports on questions raised about a comparable massive QTS data center in Georgia as the company simultaneously pursues Bessemer.

Inside Climate News finds proposed Alabama data centers including Project Marvel could collectively use more electricity than all Alabama homes combined; Alabama Power says data centers must pay the full, fair cost to serve.

projects.name: Kearney Data Center
projects.note: 368 MW; CUP discussed at Planning Commission Aug 21. Staff recommended approval.

events.summary: Planning Commission to discuss CUP; staff recommends approval.

projects.name: Sarasota County Data Center (Cattleman Road)
projects.note: Unnamed company eyed Cattleman Road; county responded with unanimous 1-year moratorium (5-0). Commissioner: 'not now, never.'

events.summary: Commission voted 5-0 for 1-year moratorium. Joins Citrus, Nassau, Hernando counties.

projects.name: Amazon Montgomery County Data Center
projects.note: Multibillion-dollar Amazon DC; announced amid statewide regulatory debate (HB 3362 failed).

events.summary: Administrative review completed for the Amazon-linked Project Green data center land-use proposal in Montgomery County near New Florence.
Montgomery County Commission approved the still-unnamed Project Green development (later confirmed as Amazon).
Montgomery County Commission approved land for two large-scale data center projects (Project Green/Amazon ~1,000 acres and Project Spade/Google ~780 acres) at the I-70/Highway 19 interchange.

Montgomery County Commission voted unanimously to approve a tax abatement framework for the AWS data center (min. $8.5B capital investment, 4-17 buildings, projected $326M-$1.5B in property tax revenue, min. 150 FT jobs at ~$85,000/yr).
A town hall on the Google/Amazon data center projects drew hundreds of residents to Montgomery County High School, with attendees voicing uncertainty and fear.

Preserve Montgomery County LLC sued Montgomery County and the Missouri DED alleging roughly a dozen Missouri Sunshine Law violations tied to the Amazon data center approval — closed-door sessions, NDAs with Amazon, improper meeting notice. Sought invalidation of the county agreements.

Missouri Reps. Wellenkamp and Costlow introduced HB 3362, the AI Infrastructure, Grid Integrity and Water Resources Protection Act, requiring large-load customers to cover grid-infrastructure costs, obtain DNR permits for large water use, and including a grid-emergency kill switch provision.

Missouri House committee held a hearing on HB 3362 with almost exclusively supportive testimony; Montgomery County resident Sylvia Kueny testified about community concerns. The bill never advanced to a floor vote.
A separate citizens group Wake Up JeffCo filed its own lawsuit challenging data-center development processes in the region.

Amazon and Gov. Kehoe announced a $10 billion AWS data center campus (~1,000 acres) in Montgomery County: 400+ direct jobs, Amazon covering 100% of grid connection costs, and over $7 million in community contributions. Announcement came while Sunshine Law litigation was still pending.
Gov. Kehoe attended a groundbreaking event for the Amazon data center project in Montgomery City.

About 100 protesters rallied in Jefferson City ahead of a data-center policy summit, citing the Amazon Montgomery County announcement and warning officials they would be voted out over inadequate corporate tax contributions.
Amazon hosted a public information open house at Montgomery County Middle School while the Missouri Rural Crisis Center held a concurrent press conference outside voicing opposition.
St. Louis Public Radio reported the Missouri legislature passed no data-center regulation this session despite HB 3362/HB 3390, and that a House Special Committee hearing is set for September 2026.
Missouri Independent reported that data-center backlash spilled into Missouri primary races, with GOP candidates demanding stronger regulation and fair tax contribution from developers.

projects.name: Microsoft Three Mile Island (Crane Clean Energy Center)
projects.note: $1.6B power purchase agreement to restart TMI Unit 1 (renamed Crane Clean Energy Center) by 2028; Microsoft will buy 100% of the 835MW nuclear output for 20 years to power its AI data centers.

events.summary: Pennsylvania anti-nuclear activists began organizing to oppose the restart, citing safety and evacuation concerns tied to the 1979 TMI-2 accident.

Constellation Energy announced a 20-year power purchase agreement with Microsoft to restart the 835 MW Three Mile Island Unit 1, renamed the Crane Clean Energy Center, to supply carbon-free power for Microsoft data centers; the deal is expected to create ~3,400 jobs and add $16 billion to Pennsylvania GDP.
Local reporting captured mixed community reactions in Londonderry Township/Dauphin County, with labor groups voicing support while some residents raised fear of another accident.
Constellation laid out its reopening timeline at a public hearing, telling regulators and residents it aimed to have Unit 1 producing power again by 2027-2028.
Constellation submitted its initial restart application to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission for Three Mile Island Unit 1 (Crane Clean Energy Center).
Constellation began evaluating the environmental impacts of the restart as part of the NRC review process, covering water use from the Susquehanna River, air quality, and spent fuel management.
Activist Gene Stilp sued Dauphin County commissioners and the Public Safety Department, alleging misuse of taxpayer funds to promote the plant restart.
The NRC formally accepted Constellation restart request for Three Mile Island Unit 1 for detailed technical review.
Residents told federal regulators the NRC review process feels like a charade, pressing concerns about safety, evacuation planning, and environmental impact at a public forum near the plant.
The NRC held a second public meeting, this one virtual, allowing community members nationwide to comment on the proposed restart of the Crane Clean Energy Center reactor.
NRC staff issued a Request for Additional Information (RAI) to Constellation as part of the technical review of the Unit 1 restart application.
Constellation submitted its response to the NRC Request for Additional Information regarding the Crane Clean Energy Center restart.
NRC docket correspondence addressed to Constellation Energy regarding the Crane Clean Energy Center restart review.
The U.S. Department of Energy closed a $1 billion loan to Constellation Energy to help finance the roughly $1.6 billion restart of Three Mile Island Unit 1/Crane Clean Energy Center.
U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright touted the $1 billion DOE loan for the Three Mile Island restart as delivering on the Trump administration nuclear energy promises.
PJM independent market monitor Monitoring Analytics filed comments with FERC opposing Constellation requested tariff waivers for the Crane restart.

FERC approved a waiver allowing Constellation to transfer 760 MW of Capacity Interconnection Rights from its Eddystone plant to the Crane Clean Energy Center, over the objection of PJM independent market monitor.
The NRC issued draft environmental assessment findings that the Crane Clean Energy Center restart would have no significant environmental impact, opening a public comment period.

Reporting noted continued community concern as the Crane nuclear plant restart progressed toward its targeted 2027 date, including concerns about reliance on the Susquehanna River amid climate-driven flood risk.

projects.name: AWS Caddo Parish
projects.note: $12B multi-site data center investment in Caddo Parish, Louisiana.

events.summary: Memorandums of purchase and sale filed for two tracts totaling over 810 acres for what became the AWS/STACK campuses — one at Resilient Technology Park in west Shreveport, the other along State Line Road near Blanchard.
Caddo Parish Commission voted in support of a PILOT incentive package to help attract the AWS data center campus.
Shreveport Metropolitan Planning Commission denied the special use permit for the then-unnamed data center project at the Resilient Technology Park campus.
Shreveport City Council voted 7-0 to overturn the Planning Commission denial and approve the special use permit for the west Shreveport data center.

Three plaintiffs filed suit in Caddo Parish District Court seeking judicial review of the City Council decision overturning the Planning Commission denial, putting the west Shreveport project in legal limbo for roughly 90 days.

Gov. Landry and Amazon publicly announced a $12 billion, multi-site AWS data center buildout across Caddo and Bossier Parishes developed with STACK Infrastructure; expected to create 540 direct jobs and support 1,710 additional FTE positions.

Amazon detailed state incentives including LED FastStart workforce training, High Impact Jobs Program, Data Center Sales Tax Exemption, plus commitments to pay 100% of its own electricity costs and invest roughly $400 million in public water infrastructure.
