AEP/SWEPCO stated that no costs associated with serving the new Amazon data centers would be passed along to existing utility ratepayers.
Local coverage confirmed the specific campus locations spanning Bossier and Caddo Parishes, including the Resilient Technology Park and Stateline Road sites.

Shreveport residents raised concerns at public meetings over the Amazon data center impact on utilities, water supply and the environment, including questions about roughly 7.5 million gallons of water per day.
Community organizers held a town hall The Truth About Data Centers drawing nearly 100 attendees opposed to the project over environmental impact, infrastructure strain and lack of oversight.

Bossier Parish Police Jury held a two-hour-plus public hearing on the final property allocation for the $6 billion Bossier campus; residents pressed officials on water usage, contamination risk, noise, and NDA use during site-selection.
Bossier Parish Police Jury formally backed the Amazon data center project, approving the property allocation.
Judge Ramon Lafitte dismissed the lawsuit challenging the City Council approval of the special use permit for the Resilient Technology Park campus, clearing the way for construction.

Reporting highlighted that Caddo Parish has no comprehensive land-use/zoning blueprint for unincorporated areas, meaning the parish cannot enforce typical land-use regulations on data center development.
Amazon and STACK held informational briefings for Bossier and Shreveport officials including public safety representatives.
Reporting detailed a proposal to freeze new data center tax breaks in Caddo Parish while officials study long-term fiscal and infrastructure effects.

Commissioner John-Paul Young introduced Resolution 53 proposing a two-year moratorium on new data center developments, expansions, and tax incentive agreements in unincorporated Caddo Parish; would not affect the AWS campus already under construction.

At a Caddo Parish Commission work session, commissioners clashed over data center oversight resolutions; an attempt to fast-track failed 8-3 and commissioners voted 11-0 to refer both measures to committee. Parish attorney warned the proposed moratorium cannot legally be enacted by resolution.

AWS announced a third data center campus for Shreveport/Resilient Technology Park, a $6 billion addition bringing total NW Louisiana investment to $18 billion; adds 210 direct jobs (up to 750 across all campuses) plus up to $400M in public water infrastructure.
Shreveport civic and business leaders characterized the additional $6 billion Amazon investment as a milestone for the region.

projects.name: Aligned Data Centers Hale County
projects.note: $5B, 540MW campus with 6 facilities in Hale County, Texas. Under construction.

events.summary: Aligned Data Centers held a community meeting at Interstate 27 and FM 54 north of Abernathy where executives addressed resident concerns about infrastructure, jobs, electricity and water use; Abernathy Mayor Harold Bufe said the city would not risk its drinking water and floated possible city annexation of the site.

Aligned Data Centers publicly announced Project Caprock, a 540 MW, 313-acre, six-facility data center campus in Hale County just outside Abernathy, projected to bring $5 billion into the regional economy.
Aligned Data Centers broke ground on Project Caprock in Hale County, with Ryan Companies as general contractor and the first building targeted for Q1 2027.

Aligned announced a partnership with Xcel Energy for Project Caprock electrical infrastructure, with Aligned building and funding the dedicated power infrastructure itself to shield local ratepayers from added costs.

Aligned said Project Caprock will use its closed-loop DeltaFlow liquid cooling system paired with air-cooled heat rejection that recirculates water, produces no wastewater, and is designed to protect the Ogallala Aquifer.
National coverage of AI data center backlash in rural Texas featured the future data center site near Abernathy as part of reporting on divisions among rural Republicans over water and power impacts.

Texas Gov. Greg Abbott directed the PUCT and ERCOT to pause new data center grid interconnections statewide pending an audit — a statewide freeze affecting new-project connections including the Texas Panhandle/South Plains region where Project Caprock sits.
Reporting noted regulators and lawmakers still lack clear data on how much water and power data centers statewide consume.
President Trump publicly criticized Gov. Abbott data center moratorium as a mistake; Abbott responded by touting cooperation with tech companies including Meta and OpenAI.
Follow-up reporting found Texas data center audit still lacked specifics on scope and methodology; ERCOT indicated the audit would begin shortly after August 20 and last several months.

projects.name: Microsoft Central Ohio Campuses
projects.note: $1B investment across 3 campuses in Central Ohio. Under construction.

events.summary: Microsoft-linked entities purchase three parcels totaling 291 acres along Refugee Road SW and Etna Parkway in Pataskala, Licking County, for $30.65 million.
Microsoft Licking County land purchases (eventually topping 700 acres across New Albany, Heath, Hebron, and Pataskala/Johnstown) first reported publicly, ahead of any formal project announcement.
AEP Ohio files an application with PUCO proposing a new large-load/data-center rate tariff, a case in which Microsoft later becomes a formal party.
The Columbus Dispatch confirms Microsoft plans to construct a $420 million, 245,000 sq ft data center on a 200-acre Beech Road site in New Albany.
New Albany City Council unanimously approves a 15-year, 100% property tax abatement for Microsoft $420 million Beech Road data center.
Microsoft formally announces a $1 billion first-phase investment in three Central Ohio data center campuses in New Albany, Heath, and Hebron (Licking County).
Ohio Tax Credit Authority approves a 15-year, 100% sales-tax exemption for Microsoft three Licking County campuses, estimated at $72.5 million in forgone state revenue.
Site clearing begins at the New Albany Beech Road campus with silt-fence installation and a construction access road built, briefly narrowing Beech Road to one lane.

Microsoft tells the Columbus Dispatch and local mayors it is pausing its $1 billion Licking County plans at New Albany, Heath, and Hebron, citing investment-strategy evaluation; says it will retain the land.

PUCO adopts AEP Ohio data-center tariff requiring large data centers (including Microsoft facilities) to pay for at least 85% of contracted electric capacity for up to 12 years, with a four-year ramp-up.
AEP Ohio new data-center tariff takes effect, requiring qualifying large-load facilities above 25 MW to pay 85% of subscribed monthly capacity.
Microsoft signs a construction contract with Ames Construction for the Hebron data center, setting a bulk-construction window of March-August 2026 targeting completion by November 2026.

Microsoft holds groundbreaking ceremonies and resumes construction at Heath and Hebron campuses after a roughly one-year pause; declines real-estate tax abatements at both, benefiting Lakewood Local School District.
Microsoft purchases an additional 43 acres at Etna Parkway and Refugee Road in Pataskala for $11.44 million, adjacent to its earlier 291-acre acquisition.
Ohio Select Committee on Data Centers begins formal legislative hearings on data center growth, water/electricity demand, tax incentives, and NDAs.

Ohio Joint Data Center Committee hears over four hours of public testimony from researchers, activists, and residents on data centers electric/water demand, environmental impact, tax incentives, and NDAs; over 50 Ohio local governments reported to have data-center moratoriums.

Microsoft senior director Daniel Brown testifies before Ohio Select Committee, announcing Microsoft will stop using NDAs with local governments and will not seek local property tax abatements at its four Licking County sites; Amazon, Google, and Meta decline similar pledges.
Ohio state Sen. Brian Chavez introduces sweeping data-center legislation on tax breaks, NDAs, water use/testing, and utility billing, drawing on Select Committee testimony.

projects.name: Microsoft Person County
projects.note: Multi-billion dollar data center campus on 1,350 acres in Person County, North Carolina.

events.summary: Person County announced Microsoft had purchased roughly 1,350 acres in Woodsdale Township for approximately $26.85 million, forming the Person County Mega Park site; the buyer identity and intended use were not disclosed at the time.
Clean Water for NC, Appalachian Voices, and Sierra Club organized a community meeting in Roxboro where residents voiced frustration over the county lack of transparency about the Microsoft project.
The Carolinian reported the deal had been roughly 18 months in the making; Person County economic development director cited expected benefits of job creation and tax-base growth.
Duke Energy signed an agreement to supply power to Microsoft and Compass North Carolina data center campuses, pushing Duke total contracted data-center load from 3 GW to 4.5 GW.

WRAL reported Microsoft moving forward with Person County data center and planning to begin formal permitting later in 2026; Microsoft pledged to pay its own way on electricity and minimize/replenish water use.

Spectrum News covered ongoing resident concerns about why county officials remained bound by an NDA even after the land purchase became public; Appalachian Voices highlighted water usage and transparency as top concerns.
WRAL surveyed how central NC counties were handling data center development pressure, situating Person County within a regional wave of local pauses and scrutiny.

A public hearing on a proposed Duke Energy base-rate hike (16-18%) was held at the Person County Courthouse; residents connected the increase to Duke gas-plant buildout for data centers and said they should not subsidize Microsoft electricity costs.
The Assembly NC published an investigative piece revealing county officials signed NDAs and were preparing for the Microsoft project well before residents were informed.
Economic development director completed the rezoning application covering the Microsoft parcels; the abstract named the parcels but did not name the client or intended use.

Microsoft hosted a community meeting in Woodsdale amid statewide AI tensions (Elon University poll found only 24% of NC residents support data centers in their community); Roxboro City Councilor Coggins said the company gave a lot of canned responses on water extraction.
Person County planning board held its public hearing on the Microsoft-related rezoning application.
Person County commissioners voted to approve the rezoning for the Microsoft data center parcels, passing with little friction under generic bureaucratic language.

projects.name: QTS / Lancium Turkey TX
projects.note: $10B+ GW-scale data center campus in Turkey, Texas.

events.summary: Lancium held a town hall in Turkey, Texas drawing dozens of residents for a three-and-a-half-hour discussion; CEO Michael McNamara answered questions.

Hall County Commissioners Court unanimously approved a property tax abatement for Lancium Clean Campus: 75% abatement phased across 10 annual increments, below the 85% Lancium had originally requested.

QTS and Lancium formally announced a joint $10B+ data center campus on Lancium Clean Campus near Turkey: up to 11 buildings across ~465 acres, 1GW grid connection, Lancium supplying dedicated solar/battery and funding 100% of energy infrastructure; closed-loop cooling designed to use no water.
Trade and local press (DatacenterDynamics, Baxtel, ABC7 Amarillo) covered the QTS/Lancium Hall County announcement, reiterating the 11-building, 465-acre, 1GW, $10B campus figures.
NewsChannel 10 reported on the project, quoting Hall County Judge Ray Powell and noting water would come from onsite wells rather than Turkey municipal supply.

Gov. Abbott ordered PUC of Texas and ERCOT to audit every data center in the interconnection queue (~1,800 projects) before further grid-connection approvals, affecting all pending Texas data center interconnections including large-load projects like Lancium Turkey campus.
Lancium issued a statement supporting Gov. Abbott transparency/accountability push, with CEO McNamara pledging verified power/water reporting, full grid-upgrade funding, and closed-loop cooling.

ABC7 Amarillo reported Hall County residents raising concerns about water usage and housing-cost strain; QTS responded closed-loop buildings would use ~50,000 gallons/month each (about five single-family homes) and most workers housed on-site.
QTS and Lancium held a community engagement meeting at Valley High School (5:30-7:30 PM) to address resident concerns on tax revenue, school/workforce partnerships, and infrastructure support.

projects.name: OpenAI Stargate Doña Ana County
projects.note: Part of Stargate. GW-scale data center campus in Doña Ana County, New Mexico.

events.summary: OpenAI, SoftBank, and Oracle announce the $500 billion Stargate joint venture to build massive U.S. AI data center infrastructure.
New Mexico Governor Michelle Lujan Grisham and BorderPlex Digital Assets Chairman Lanham Napier jointly announce plans for a large digital infrastructure campus in Santa Teresa, Dona Ana County.

Dona Ana Board of County Commissioners votes to terminate the joint powers agreement that created the Camino Real Regional Utility Authority, affecting local water/utility governance ahead of the data center buildout.
Construction begins on the Project Jupiter data center campus along NM-136 near the Santa Teresa Port of Entry in Dona Ana County.

Dona Ana County commissioners approve an unprecedented $165 billion industrial revenue bond to help finance Project Jupiter; the vote draws protests outside the County Government Center in Las Cruces.
Project Jupiter is officially named as one of five sites in the $500 billion Stargate Project, the OpenAI/Oracle/SoftBank AI infrastructure initiative.
New Mexico Environmental Law Center files a lawsuit on behalf of residents challenging the Dona Ana County commissioners funding ordinance approvals for Project Jupiter.
Air quality permit applications for Project Jupiter are filed with the New Mexico Environment Department, showing potential emissions of up to 14 million tons of carbon dioxide annually.
BorderPlex Digital Assets presents renewable energy plans targeting 500 MW of renewables by 2028 and 1,000 MW by 2032 to offset Project Jupiter power draw.
Forbes profiles the developers and scale of Project Jupiter, detailing plans for four data center buildings, microgrids, and phased power buildout from 700-900 MW toward 4 GW.

Oracle, BorderPlex, and Bloom Energy announce Project Jupiter will switch from natural gas turbines to a 2.45 GW Bloom Energy solid-oxide fuel cell microgrid, cutting NOx emissions roughly 92% and using negligible water, after community pushback.
New Mexico Environment Department schedules an October 19 public hearing on Project Jupiter air quality permit application.
Food and Water Watch publishes an analysis arguing Project Jupiter exemplifies Big Tech playbook for pushing through data centers with limited transparency.

Dona Ana County commissioners meeting on Project Jupiter turns disruptive: three protesters are arrested/ejected, Oracle VP pledges 7,000 peak construction jobs and no public drinking water use, and state Rep. Rubio says public comment was suppressed.
Project Jupiter air quality permit public hearing is rescheduled from October to September.
New Mexico Environmental Law Center reports the Project Jupiter air quality permit hearing date was moved again amid disputes over scheduling.
Center for Biological Diversity asks the New Mexico Supreme Court to pause Project Jupiter air quality permit hearing, disputing the rescheduled hearing date.

projects.name: PA Data Center Partners Cumberland County
projects.note: $15B, 1.35 GW across 3 campuses in Cumberland County, Pennsylvania.

events.summary: A draft comprehensive zoning ordinance submitted to the Cumberland County Planning Department by Middlesex Township attorney, ahead of the data center overlay process.
Township attorney submits a standalone Data Center Overlay District Amendment; Cumberland County Planning Department issues its review report on the overlay map and text.

Middlesex Township Board of Supervisors unanimously approves Ordinance No. 3-2025, creating a 694-715 acre Data Center Overlay District making hyperscale data centers a permitted by-right use, sharply limiting future public hearings.

PA Data Center Partners and PowerHouse Data Centers announce the $15 billion, 1.35 GW PAX-1 three-campus hyperscale complex on ~700 acres in Middlesex Township at the PA Energy and Innovation Summit at Carnegie Mellon, attended by President Trump.
PA Data Center Partners/PowerHouse JV paid roughly $44 million to acquire the Middlesex Township land for the project.
Middlesex Township Planning Commission discusses the PAX-1 Master Sketch Plan; no official action taken.
Middlesex Township Planning Commission approves the PPL substation laydown-yard plan for the project, with conditions.

Residents formally ask the Middlesex Township Board to reclassify data centers as conditional use rather than by-right; the board denies the request and approves a revised comprehensive zoning ordinance.
Developer holds a public outreach meeting for residents on the PAX-1 project.

Middlesex Authority reports analysis finding roughly 910,000 gallons/day of unused peak water capacity, of which 400,000 gallons/day would be reserved for PAX-1, leaving over 500,000 gallons/day for other development.
Middlesex Township Planning Commission votes to recommend approval of subdivision plans splitting the 693-acre tract into three data-center campuses plus a substation parcel.
Water rights/allocation for the PAX-1 project formally secured with the Middlesex Authority.
Middlesex Township Board unanimously approves construction of a 450 MW electrical substation; PPL Electric Utilities confirms it can meet the full 1.35 GW peak demand with planned upgrades.
Construction resumes on the $15 billion PAX-1 project following the substation approval.
Two weeks of scheduled underground construction blasting begin at the PAX-1 site, twice daily on weekdays; nearby Country Manor West residents report feeling and hearing the blasts.

State Rep. Joe Webster begins advocating for new state oversight of data center projects including legislation requiring water-usage disclosure, amid resident complaints about PAX-1 construction noise, blasting, and well-water impacts.

A planned town hall on data centers with State Rep. Barb Gleim (R-Cumberland) is canceled after overwhelming resident interest exceeded the space; residents say it felt like officials did not want to hear their concerns.

Cumberland County Planning Department issues a review report recommending Middlesex Township deny an expansion of the data center overlay district and update its outdated 2003 comprehensive plan before amending zoning further.

Cumberland County Planning Commission, Dickinson College, and CAEDC host a virtual data-center informational session drawing 230 pre-registration questions and 118 live, reflecting intense public interest.
Pennsylvania House votes 197-5 to pass HB 2198 repealing the Computer Data Center Equipment sales-tax incentive, projected to cost $188.4 million in FY2026-27 growing to $517 million by 2030.
Pennsylvania Senate passes HB 1667 containing the same data center tax incentive repeal by a vote of 44-6.

Middlesex Township supervisors cancel a planned vote to approve final construction of a PAX-1 building after more than 150 residents pack the municipal building beyond capacity, creating a fire hazard; rescheduled to August 19 at a school gym.

Cumberland County residents organized by Neighbors Against PAX-1 rally against the data center, arguing the developer helped write the zoning ordinance in a way that handcuffs the township ability to impose conditions.

Ten Middlesex residents (Neighbors Against PAX-1 / Stop PAX-1) file a substantive validity/spot-zoning legal challenge alleging the 2025 data center overlay ordinance was effectively written by PAX-1 developers and approved via illegal spot zoning.

Opponents file a separate appeal with the PA Environmental Hearing Board challenging a stormwater permit for the PAX-1 site, arguing it was written for a 58-house residential subdivision rather than a hyperscale data center.

Gov. Shapiro signs a statewide executive order restricting data center development: requiring local approval for state permits, removing data centers from fast-track permitting, mandating CBAs, binding environmental/transparency commitments, and that projects secure their own electricity supply.
Rescheduled Middlesex Township supervisors meeting on PAX-1 building approval postponed a second time (moved to September 2) after a township official suffers a medical episode during the meeting.

projects.name: Hut 8 / Google West Feliciana Parish
projects.note: $10B, 1,000 MW data center campus in West Feliciana Parish, Louisiana.

events.summary: West Feliciana Parish President Kenny Havard teased a major economic development announcement at a parish council meeting, later revealed to be tied to the data center project land assembly.

West Feliciana Parish sold 107 acres of surplus land near the old paper mill to M/V Industrial LLC for $500,000 ($4,672/acre) — later at the center of a land-deal controversy tied to the data center site assembly.
Havard announced the parish had sold the 107-acre industrial park site for $500,000 for what he described as a project that would be a major economic boost.

West Feliciana Parish officials unanimously approved rezoning/development of the AI data center; Phase 1 includes two 450,000-sq-ft buildings. Officials flagged traffic-safety concerns and Hut 8 said closed-loop cooling would avoid heavy water consumption.
Parish council approved the $2.5 billion Hut 8 data center project with an aggressive timeline to build.

M/V Industrial LLC finalized purchase of additional nearby parcels for millions of dollars, then the same day resold those properties to Hut 8 for the data center site — a transaction central to later corruption allegations.

WBRZ investigative report: Port Commission members alleged Parish President Havard and Port Commission President Grezaffi improperly profited from the 2023 land sale (M/V Industrial LLC tied to Grezaffi Cedar Management Company), claiming the parish was defrauded of roughly $11.5 million. Ethics complaint filed the next day.
West Feliciana Parish Council voted 3-2 to pass a resolution supporting a state bill to dissolve the West Feliciana Port Commission, amid the land-deal dispute.
Hut 8 broke ground on the $2.5 billion (Phase I) River Bend data center on a 611-acre parcel off LA 964; first building targeted for completion by end of 2025, second before end of 2026.

Hut 8 signed a 15-year, $7.0 billion lease (up to $17.7B with renewals) with Fluidstack for 245 MW at River Bend, with Google (Alphabet) providing two financial backstops. Anthropic is the ultimate compute user via Fluidstack.

Hut 8, Anthropic, and Fluidstack jointly announced a multi-gigawatt AI infrastructure partnership (245 MW up to 2,295 MW); Louisiana Economic Development announced Hut 8 selection of the site for a $10 billion Phase I investment scalable to 1,000+ MW, backed by Entergy Louisiana (330 MW initial).
Hut 8 River Bend projected to generate $90 million annually for West Feliciana Parish (versus $41M current tax revenue) under a 30-year PILOT agreement with the parish Industrial Development Board.
State legislation (HB466) introduced that would let West Feliciana Industrial Development Board rebate property taxes to residents/businesses from the anticipated data center revenue windfall.

Parish officials outlined plans to replace West Feliciana 1948 jail (39-bed expanding to ~150) using data-center PILOT revenue; first prepayment anticipated around July 2026, full annual payments (~$90M/yr for 15 years) expected once project completes late 2027.
Hut 8 committed $16 million to expand West Feliciana water infrastructure (new well, ~8 miles of water main) to be transferred to the parish at no taxpayer cost, serving 4,000+ households.
Jacobs began formal EPCM work on the $10 billion River Bend campus, partnering with Vertiv on critical infrastructure; financed up to 85% via project-level debt from J.P. Morgan and Goldman Sachs.

West Feliciana Parish Council and Industrial Development Board approved a cooperative endeavor agreement accepting a $10 million advance on Hut 8 future PILOT payments, split $5.3M to school board, $3.9M to parish government, and $800,000 to sheriff office.
Hut 8 held a hiring event and community open house at West Feliciana Parish High School for River Bend jobs.

projects.name: Compass Datacenters Meridian
projects.note: $10B, 500MW campus with 8 facilities in Meridian, Mississippi. Under construction.

events.summary: Mississippi State University and state leaders publicly welcomed Compass Datacenters arrival in Meridian.

Compass Datacenters announced plans to build an eight-building, 500MW hyperscale campus in the I-20/59 industrial park in Lauderdale County (Meridian), representing a $10 billion investment. Gov. Reeves called it a monumental economic development win.
Meridian Star editorial credits months of closed-door discussions between EMBDC, Lauderdale County Supervisors, City of Meridian, and Mississippi Power for landing the Compass project.
Compass Datacenters held its official groundbreaking ceremony near the I-20/I-59 corridor in Lauderdale County, attended by Gov. Reeves, PSC Commissioner Stamps, and Compass VP Katie Hancock.

Mississippi Development Authority certified Compass as a data center operator, granting 10-year state income/franchise tax exemptions plus sales/use tax exemption on construction materials, equipment, and software/hardware replacements.
Mississippi Public Service Commission approved the special electric service contract between Mississippi Power and Compass Datacenters Jan I, LLC, clearing the way for ~500MW of supply to the campus.

Mississippi Senate unanimously passed SB 3168, updating the state Data Center Enterprise incentive program (raising investment thresholds, adding an electricity tax exemption, allowing automatic 10-year extensions).

Center for Economic Accountability named Mississippi Compass Datacenters/Lauderdale County tax-break package the nation Worst Economic Development Deal of the Year for 2025, citing the length and breadth of tax exemptions versus minimal disclosed local benefit.

Compass held a lunch and learn informational session at the MSU Riley Center; residents raised concerns about rising electricity and water bills, and Compass VP Sarah Ridgely responded the campus uses closed-loop water cooling.
Lauderdale County officials issued a statement strongly supporting the Compass project as transformational, citing 1,000+ construction jobs and hundreds of permanent jobs.

Mississippi Legislature AI Task Force held a two-day hearing on data center impacts; Compass SVP Brent Collard testified the company invested $300 million in Meridian grid infrastructure and created 6,400 long-term jobs, while other testimony raised statewide concerns about noise, air pollution, and water draw.

Compass and Meridian Community College launched Mississippi first data center workforce training program (14-week MEI Data Center Pathway) with Compass funding full-tuition scholarships for an inaugural cohort of 12 students.

projects.name: Google Berkeley County
projects.note: $9B multi-site data center investment in Berkeley County, South Carolina. Under construction.

events.summary: Google announces plans to construct a data center complex in Berkeley County, SC (Mount Holly Commerce Park, Moncks Corner) — its first South Carolina site, initial investment around $600 million.
Google announces plans to build a second building at the Berkeley County site.
Fee-in-Lieu of Tax (FILOT) agreement formalized, cutting Google property-tax assessment rate from 10.5% to 4% and locking it in for up to 50 years with an 80% rebate on the fee.
Google announces a further $600 million expansion, bringing cumulative Berkeley County investment to about $1.2 billion.
Google receives a state permit to withdraw up to 183 million gallons per year of groundwater from the Charleston/Middendorf aquifer.
Google reapplies to DHEC seeking to roughly triple its groundwater withdrawal permit to about 549 million gallons per year.

Berkeley County approves a tax-incentive package for a $600 million expansion (entity Maguro Enterprises), maintaining the 4% assessment/80% rebate FILOT structure; investment total reaches $2.4 billion.
Google reapplies to DHEC for the 549-million-gallon-per-year groundwater withdrawal permit from the Middendorf aquifer.
DHEC issues a draft permit allowing withdrawal of 549 million gallons of groundwater per year, drawing formal objections from the Coastal Conservation League and local water utilities.

Google, DHEC, the Coastal Conservation League and SELC reach a final agreement imposing tougher conditions: Google must treat groundwater as a last resort, develop alternative sources, and report usage quarterly.
A Google affiliate (Arum Composites LLC) purchases roughly 143 acres across five parcels in Berkeley County for about $28.5 million.
Google seeks a land-disturbance permit for its second data center site in rural Dorchester County (Pine Hill Business Campus).

Google announces a combined $3.3 billion investment in SC: $2 billion for two new Dorchester County campuses and $1.3 billion to expand Berkeley County; includes $2.2 million for environmental initiatives.
Groundbreaking ceremony held in Dorchester County with Governor McMaster; each new site expected to employ about 100 workers, existing Berkeley County site employs roughly 900.
Public input meeting on emergency generators for the Pine Hill campus; about eight residents raised concerns over air quality, traffic, wetland impacts, and transparency.
Google announces a new $9 billion investment through 2027 to expand Berkeley County and continue Dorchester County construction — the largest single investment in South Carolina history.
Analysis examines whether Google $9 billion SC buildout is a net boon or burden for host communities, covering tax-incentive costs versus benefits.
SC Daily Gazette reports South Carolina data centers received a combined $828 million in state tax breaks on electricity and computer-equipment purchases in the prior year.

projects.name: Google West Memphis
projects.note: $4B, 1,178-acre campus with 5 buildings in West Memphis, Arkansas. Under construction.

events.summary: Groot LLC, a Google-linked entity, paid $16.5 million to buy roughly 1,117 acres of agricultural land on Bollinger Road in West Memphis, Crittenden County.

West Memphis City Council unanimously approved a MOU, development agreement, and PILOT incentive package with Groot LLC for a project valued at up to $10 billion, with potential for up to $50 billion in personal-property tax abatements over 30 years.
Entergy Arkansas and Google jointly sought Arkansas Public Service Commission approval of a special electricity rate contract to power the West Memphis data center.
Reporting confirmed Google (via Groot LLC) as the company behind the planned $10 billion, five-building data center campus on 1,178 acres south of Bollinger Road, dubbed Project Pyramid.

Google, Governor Sarah Sanders, and state/local officials formally announced a $4 billion AI/cloud data center project in West Memphis — Google first data center in Arkansas — with a $25 million Energy Impact Fund for low-income households in Crittenden County.

Entergy Arkansas announced it would power the Google project with a 600 MW Cypress Solar project and 350 MW of battery storage, with Google saying the deal would deliver over $1.1 billion in net benefits to Entergy customers.

Arkansas PSC held a hearing on the special rate contract between Entergy and Google; the public was asked to leave during portions covering confidential contract details, drawing transparency criticism.

Arkansas PSC approved Entergy special rate contract with Google but denied the utility requested ratemaking treatment and deferred a decision on investment tax credit treatment for the Cypress Solar facility.
Arkansas Advocate reported state officials were largely declining to scrutinize fiscal and environmental tradeoffs of the data center boom out of fear of losing investment to other states.
Arkansas PSC issued a follow-up order reversing itself to allow investment tax credits from the Cypress Solar facility to be used in pricing under the Google contract.
Google began actively hiring for electrical engineer and facilities technician roles at the West Memphis data center, which remained under construction with an expected 18-24 month build timeline.
Reporting revealed Google and Entergy were keeping the full terms of their energy rate contract sealed/confidential, raising transparency concerns among ratepayer advocates.
Reporting detailed that bond issuances tied to the West Memphis Google data center PILOT financing could total as much as $60 billion in permanent financing authority over the deal 30-year term.
At an Arkansas PSC hearing on Entergy proposed residential rate increase, speakers including the Little Rock NAACP chapter head cited the sealed Google contract as evidence of a lack of transparency.

projects.name: Applied Digital Harwood ND
projects.note: $3B, 280MW data center in Harwood, North Dakota. Under construction.

events.summary: Applied Digital announced Polaris Forge 2, a $3 billion, 280MW AI data center campus on 900+ contracted acres southeast of Harwood, ND, with plans to break ground in September 2025.
About 300 residents attended a town hall at the Harwood Community Center; some shouted when is the vote? and accused the town of having sold out.
Community members voiced anger and pressed for more disclosure, citing concerns about transparency in the approval process.
City of Fargo moved to annex roughly 800 acres near Harwood including the proposed data center site; Applied Digital said it would formally protest the annexation.
Harwood City Council voted unanimously on first reading to rezone roughly 320 acres from agricultural to light industrial, after a contentious session with public shouting.
Harwood City Council gave final approval to rezone the 320-acre site in about 25 minutes at a special meeting, even as Fargo continued to pursue annexation.
Construction crews observed breaking ground on the Polaris Forge 2 site near Harwood.

Applied Digital announced a roughly $5 billion, 15-year, 200MW AI factory lease with an unnamed US-based investment-grade hyperscaler (later reported as Oracle) at Polaris Forge 2, with right of first refusal on an additional 800MW.

Reporting revealed Harwood and Fargo mayors had signed NDAs with Applied Digital covering project details, raising open-records concerns and prompting draft state legislation to ban such NDAs by public officials.
Harwood City Council voted unanimously to reject a draft agreement proposed by Fargo that would have set conditions in exchange for dropping its annexation attempt.
Fargo City Commission voted unanimously to cancel its annexation of roughly 300 acres including the data center site and voted 4-1 to send a separate disputed annexation into mediation with Harwood.
Dakota Resource Council held a public meeting on the Harwood data center drawing about 100 attendees; the group said it wants projects to be transparent and beneficial to host communities.
Applied Digital closed a $2.15 billion private offering of 6.750% senior secured notes (maturing 2031) to fund construction of roughly 200MW at the Harwood campus.
Reporting detailed Applied Digital backing of the Agassiz Transmission Line and Substation project with Minnkota Power Cooperative to deliver the 280MW needed for the Harwood campus.

Minnkota disclosed the cost of the Agassiz transmission line rose from about $75 million to $110 million due to tight timelines and tariffs; Applied Digital will cover the full cost with no charge to other customers.
North Dakota Public Service Commission approved the $110 million Agassiz Transmission Line and Substation, targeting operational by fall 2026.

Statewide reporting examined the lack of ND state-level siting authority for data centers, noting the PSC has virtually no say over location, and a failed 2025 bill (HB 1427) that would have granted it.
Applied Digital confirmed it was expanding its ND footprint and eyeing Oliver County for a third data center campus.
Harwood residents still felt left in the dark about the data center months after approval, citing the town NDA-driven negotiation process as an example of insufficient transparency.

projects.name: CyrusOne Fairfield
projects.note: $1.5B, 760MW campus with 3 buildings in Fairfield, Texas. Under construction.

events.summary: Freestone County Commissioners held a public hearing and unanimously approved Reinvestment Zone Number 12 (C1 Freestone, LLC Data Center, a CyrusOne affiliate) on 507 acres near the Calpine plant, with a minimum $600 million initial improvement and a 10-year, $850,000/year payment-in-lieu-of-taxes agreement.

Constellation's Calpine unit and CyrusOne announced a Powered Land Capabilities agreement supplying 380MW for Phase 1 of a new data center adjacent to the Freestone Energy Center, with an exclusive option for an additional 380MW in Phase 2 (760MW total).
A public notice regarding the data center project and upcoming county hearing was published in the Freestone County Times.

A Change.org petition titled "Ban Data Centers in Freestone County" was started, citing water, noise and light pollution, rising power costs, and health/traffic impacts; it drew hundreds of signatures ahead of the county's June hearings.

A Freestone County Commissioners Court meeting drew an overflow crowd (relocated to the District Courtroom) with 15+ residents raising concerns about permanent water loss, noise, health effects, and lack of transparency; resident Toni Abram asked for a 1-2 year pause, and the court scheduled a special meeting for June 10 and a public hearing for June 17.
CyrusOne held a groundbreaking ceremony for its Freestone County data center campus with County Judge Lloyd Lane, Fairfield Mayor Bobby Nichols, Calpine, and contractor Rogers-O'Brien Construction.

A special Freestone County Commissioners Court meeting was held at which CyrusOne presented information addressing resident concerns, citing a closed-loop water system (~1,000 gallons/day per building), 45-55 decibel noise levels, about 40 jobs per building, and a 2030 carbon-neutral goal.

At a public hearing on a proposed Phase 2 tax abatement, roughly 30 residents voiced opposition over noise, water pollution, utility bills, and transparency; CyrusOne subsequently rescinded its tax abatement request for Phase 2, and County Judge Lloyd Lane said the abatement agreement had been the county's only leverage over the project.

CyrusOne filed permits with the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation for a three-building, $1.5 billion, 760MW data center campus (buildings DFW20A, DFW20B, DFW20C) on FM 488 in Fairfield, targeting completion by the end of August 2027.

projects.name: CyrusOne Bosque County
projects.note: $1.2B, 190MW Phase 1 data center in Bosque County, Texas. Under construction.

events.summary: Bosque County commissioners approved a tax abatement for CyrusOne's data center project and for Calpine Corporation's related energy expansion, backing the $1.2 billion initiative (financed in part by BlackRock and KKR).

CyrusOne registered its DFW10 project with the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation: a $750 million, 250,000-square-foot single-story data center with a two-story office component at 557 CR 3610, Whitney.

Calpine and CyrusOne announced a new 190-megawatt powered-land agreement to serve a new CyrusOne data center adjacent to Calpine's Thad Hill Energy Center in Bosque County, with the facility under construction and targeted for Q4 2026 operation.
Calpine and CyrusOne announced Phase 2 of their powered-land agreement, adding 210MW to the original 190MW commitment for a combined 400-megawatt deal at the Bosque County campus.

CyrusOne filed Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation applications for two additional facilities at the Whitney site, DFW17B ($500M, 249,090 sq ft) and DFW17C ($430M, 93,319 sq ft with an office component), expanding the Bosque County campus.
Houston Chronicle reported on CyrusOne's newly filed $430 million, 93,319-square-foot data center building at FM56 and CR3610A in Whitney, part of the expanding Bosque County campus.
The Waco Bridge published an analysis of water, power, and political challenges facing the CyrusOne/Calpine data center project region, including the Bosque County campus.

Bosque County commissioners hosted a town hall/special commissioners-court session at the Clifton ISD Performing Arts Center where CyrusOne president John Hatem told roughly 60 residents the 400MW data center uses closed-loop cooling and would not draw down Lake Whitney; residents raised concerns about Middle Trinity aquifer depletion, with one warning the county could be "out of groundwater in 30 to 35 years."

The Waco Bridge reported on the Lake Whitney data center town hall, noting officials' projection of a 120% county tax-base increase (about $70 million over 30 years) and continuing resident skepticism over water use.
CyrusOne topped out the first building (DFW10) at its Bosque County campus, with initial fit-out of DFW10 and DFW11 targeted for October 2026 and August 2027 respectively.

A standing-room-only Bosque County Commissioners Court meeting on proposed data-center tax abatements drew strong resident opposition over rural infrastructure, water use, noise, energy demand, and fire-safety preparedness; commissioners took no action and set a June 17 deadline for revisions.

projects.name: CyrusOne Aurora
projects.note: $1B+, 40MW initial data center in Aurora, Illinois. Under construction.

events.summary: CyrusOne LP acquired CME Group Chicago-Aurora I data center in Aurora, Illinois for $131.1 million, establishing CyrusOne original Aurora campus.
Aurora Finance Committee recommended approval of a Memorandum of Reimbursement between the city and CyrusOne for the Bilter Road data center property.

Aurora officials confirmed negotiations with CyrusOne to rezone 30 acres on Bilter Road for a new data center building, while the city sought to recapture part of the $9.3 million it spent on the I-88/Eola interchange in 2008.
Aurora City Council approved the Memorandum of Reimbursement with CyrusOne for the 2725 Bilter Road site.

Governor JB Pritzker, Aurora Mayor Richard Irvin, and CyrusOne CEO Eric Schwartz held a groundbreaking ceremony for a $350 million, two-building (446,000 sq ft), 40 MW data center campus on Bilter Road, expected to open in early 2026.

Coverage confirmed the project was approved under the Illinois Department of Commerce and Economic Opportunity data center investment incentive program and includes a Project Labor Agreement with IBEW.
Equipment repairs at the Aurora CyrusOne data center required extended backup generator use over multiple days, producing noise nearby residents called unlivable.
CyrusOne installed a temporary generator sound wall at its Aurora facility amid escalating resident noise complaints.
The City of Aurora issued code-enforcement citations against CyrusOne over noise from backup generators and rooftop chillers at the Diehl/Eola Road data center.

Aurora City Council unanimously enacted a 180-day citywide moratorium on new data center and warehouse development applications and expansions, driven substantially by resident backlash over CyrusOne noise complaints.
Aurora and CyrusOne signed a legal agreement resolving the May 2025 noise citations, setting a compliance timeline for permanent generator and chiller sound fixes and a $40,000 fine.

A cooling-plant failure at the CyrusOne-owned CME Group data center in Aurora caused temperatures to exceed 100F and halted CME derivatives trading for nearly 10 hours, disrupting global futures and options markets.

As its 180-day moratorium expired, Aurora City Council approved strict siting and performance rules on new data centers: mandatory noise/water/sound studies, daytime/nighttime decibel caps (56/46 dB), and generators/chillers set back 1,500 feet from homes.

Residents near the CyrusOne Aurora data center said noise (measured around 80 decibels) continued disrupting daily life despite the company rooftop sound wall and ComEd-partnered generator-runtime reductions.

Public radio coverage examined how Aurora (centered on the CyrusOne facility) and DeKalb have taken different regulatory approaches to data center noise, water and energy impacts amid continued resident complaints.

projects.name: QTS Dane County
projects.note: Multi-billion dollar, 750MW renewable-powered data center campus in Dane County, Wisconsin.

events.summary: QTS Data Centers began exploring a multi-building data center campus on a 615-acre property in the Town of Vienna, Dane County, holding a public drop-in meeting to introduce the concept.
Local residents and officials raised early questions about the scale, water use, and energy demand of the proposed QTS data center campus in rural Dane County.
Dane County energy office director told Madison sustainability committee the proposed Vienna data center could use about 2.5 times the electricity that all of Dane County currently consumes.
QTS planned to submit a formal zoning/annexation application to the DeForest Village Board, triggering village staff due diligence with outside legal and development experts.
QTS and UW-Madison announced a $1.5 million Advancing Data Center Sustainability research partnership with the Nelson Institute for Environmental Studies, funding 14 faculty research projects.

QTS announced a $12 billion, up-to-1,600-acre data center campus in Dane County (Town of Vienna/DeForest), partnering with the Building Trades Council for up to 5,000 union construction jobs and pledging a $50 million community commitment.
More than four hours of public comment at a packed DeForest Village Hall meeting drew opposition to the QTS annexation; a citizen petition sought to require large annexations to go to referendum.
Madison Common Council approved a temporary one-year moratorium on zoning approvals for new data centers larger than 10,000 square feet.

DeForest village staff recommended the Village Board reject QTS annexation petition, concluding the data center proposal was not feasible in DeForest after QTS declined pre-annexation requirements including a 70%-renewable energy commitment.
QTS withdrew its data center project from consideration in the Village of DeForest following staff recommendation against annexation and sustained community opposition.
Alliant Energy adjusted plans tied to the QTS Greater Madison project as the DeForest annexation collapsed, having previously committed to developing 750 MW of renewable generation.
The DeForest Village Board voted unanimously 7-0 to reject QTS petition to annex nearly 1,600 acres of Town of Vienna farmland, formally ending the DeForest route for the project.
Democratic state lawmakers proposed a statewide data center moratorium bill and held a day of action, citing the DeForest/QTS fight as a driver of the broader Wisconsin data center policy debate.
The Town of Westport (Dane County) enacted a one-year moratorium restricting new data centers to no more than 10,000 square feet, part of a wave of local moratoriums following the QTS controversy.
A resolution was introduced on the Dane County Board establishing an 18-month moratorium on receiving or issuing zoning permits for hyperscale data centers in unincorporated areas.
The Dane County Board of Supervisors unanimously approved an 18-month moratorium on zoning permits for hyperscale data centers in unincorporated county areas, running until December 2027.

projects.name: Meta Beaver Dam
projects.note: $1B hyperscale data center in Beaver Dam, Wisconsin.

events.summary: Beaver Dam city council created a tax incremental financing (TID) district to help fund infrastructure development for what was then an unnamed data center project.

Beaver Dam Area Development Corp. and the city publicly disclosed they were working with an unnamed company on a potential data center project, and the city council voted to approve it ahead of Meta being named.

Meta, Governor Tony Evers, and state/local officials announced a $1 billion, 700,000+ sq ft AI-optimized data center campus on roughly 500 acres in Beaver Dam Commerce Park — Meta first Wisconsin facility, expected online in 2027.
Meta said it will underwrite nearly $200 million in energy infrastructure investment (substations, transmission lines, network upgrades) coordinated with Alliant Energy.
Meta officially broke ground on the $1 billion AI-driven data center campus in Beaver Dam; the facility will use dry-cooling technology intended to eliminate operational cooling water demand.
Meta published details on its 30th global data center, citing community benefits commitments and a wetlands restoration effort tied to the Beaver Dam project.
Residents at groundbreaking-related coverage raised questions about the project transparency, following revelations that the deal had been developed via shell companies and nondisclosure agreements.

WEDC estimated the project would generate up to 1,000 skilled-trade construction jobs at peak and more than 100 permanent jobs, alongside eligibility for a sales tax exemption on construction materials.
Midwest Environmental Advocates sued the Wisconsin Public Service Commission after it denied a public-records request for unredacted electrical load projections tied to Meta Beaver Dam data center.
Local news reported on the Midwest Environmental Advocates lawsuit against the PSC over secrecy surrounding the Beaver Dam data center projected energy demand.
Investigative reporting found at least four Wisconsin communities, including Beaver Dam, had signed nondisclosure/secrecy agreements during negotiations for billion-dollar data center projects.
Oppidan Investment Co. proposed a second, smaller ~90,000 sq ft edge data center on a 13+ acre city-owned lot near Meta campus — a separate project not affiliated with Meta.
Community members organized a volunteer town hall in Beaver Dam to discuss impacts of Meta AI data center on the local community.
Sierra Club released analyses finding overwhelming public opposition to Wisconsin data centers statewide, citing Beaver Dam-area concerns among the evidence.

Beaver Dam Common Council approved a resolution authorizing a development and sale agreement for the second (Oppidan) data center, expanded TID 7 boundaries, and rezoned the parcel from residential to light industrial.
A Beaver Dam resident living near the Meta construction site reported the creek running through her property had gone dry, surged unpredictably, turned milky, and tested positive for heavy metals.
At a Beaver Dam city council meeting, at least 14 residents spoke in opposition citing environmental impacts, lack of transparent public input, and wildlife/water concerns.

Wisconsin PSC approved Alliant Energy rate contract for Meta Beaver Dam data center (~220 MW demand) but sharply criticized the secretive black-box negotiation process involving NDAs, redacted filings, and corporate pseudonyms, ordering Alliant to develop a standard rate structure for future large-load customers.
Coverage noted that in the PSC proceeding, 93% of verbal public comments and 85% of written comments argued data centers should pay 100% of their own costs rather than shifting costs to ratepayers.
RENEW Wisconsin reported the PSC modified and approved the Alliant-Meta data center contract, requiring additional reporting, a cost-of-service study, and an incremental cost analysis going forward.

projects.name: Microsoft Catawba County
projects.note: $1B multi-site data center investment in Catawba County, North Carolina. Under construction.

events.summary: Catawba County, the Cities of Conover and Hickory, the Town of Maiden, and the Catawba County EDC jointly announced Microsoft plan to invest a minimum of $1 billion in four data centers over 10 years, creating at least 50 jobs.
Coverage detailed the incentive package: performance-based tax breaks of 50% real property tax and 85% personal property tax over 10 years, across roughly 670 acres in Conover, Hickory, and Maiden.
Microsoft broke ground on the Lyle Creek campus (Project Agate) in Conover on NC Highway 16, planned for up to five data center buildings.
Site construction began on the Maiden-area data center (Boyd Farms site, Project Yoga), with Morgan Construction Company starting clearing and grading work.
Microsoft paused construction across its Catawba County data center campuses; the halt lasted roughly 10 months, with the company not publicly detailing the reason.
Satellite monitoring detected re-mobilization activity at Microsoft Lyle Creek, Boyd Farm, and Stover North campuses in Catawba County in January-February 2026.

Microsoft sent a letter to the City of Hickory stating it intends to forgo the tax rebates promised in the 2022 incentive agreement, opting to pay full property taxes under its Community-First Infrastructure initiative.

Microsoft resumed construction on its $1B Catawba County project after a roughly 10-month pause; building permits secured for sites in Conover, Hickory, Maiden, and Newton valued at $909 million, with completion obligations extending to 2032.

Catawba County, the Cities of Conover and Hickory, the Town of Maiden, and the EDC issued a joint statement defending the Microsoft project amid rising community questions, citing Microsoft tax commitment and projected water use of about 1% of Hickory daily capacity.

Residents near the Conover construction site reported ongoing noise and dust; neighboring landowners voiced opposition to the loss of rural land even as county officials touted job creation and minimal water impact.

Microsoft reported its Catawba County data centers will use far less water than originally estimated, citing a 75-80% cut in projected peak water demand and 85-90% cut in wastewater demand since 2022, attributing this to closed-loop liquid cooling.

projects.name: Microsoft La Porte
projects.note: $1B, 245,000 sq ft data center in La Porte, Indiana. Under construction.

events.summary: Gov. Eric Holcomb and Microsoft announced a $1 billion investment to build a 245,000 sq ft data center on 489 acres at Radius Industrial Park in La Porte, Indiana, projected to create up to 200 jobs by 2032.
The Indiana Economic Development Corporation committed a 35-year (extendable to 45-year) data center sales tax credit tied to a minimum $1 billion capital investment at the La Porte site.

Microsoft President Brad Smith unveiled a national Community-First AI Infrastructure Plan pledging Microsoft would no longer seek local property tax abatements — a policy shift that prompted renegotiation of the La Porte tax deal.
Microsoft began site preparation work on the La Porte campus, with the first three data center buildings under construction through end of 2027 and full buildout expected by 2029.

La Porte and the school corporation approved a revised tax agreement in which Microsoft will pay its full property tax obligation, with 15% dedicated to La Porte Community School Corporation for 20 years.

La Porte City Council held a hearing on annexing more than 1,000 acres of farmland adjacent to the existing Microsoft site for a second data center campus; officials cited a lack of transparency while some residents supported the jobs.

Microsoft held a community information session at the La Porte Civic Auditorium attended by hundreds; residents raised concerns about water usage, noise (including low-frequency vibrations), lighting/visual impact, and being excluded from earlier decisions.
LaPorte County commissioners voted unanimously to advance a new data center ordinance setting setbacks, noise limits, and water-usage caps and restricting data centers to industrial-zoned land.
The La Porte Plan Commission approved rezoning roughly 1,300 acres near Boyd Boulevard and U.S. 35 from agricultural to manufacturing use for Microsoft expansion.

La Porte Common Council unanimously approved final annexation and rezoning of more than 1,000 additional acres in Pleasant Township for light industrial/manufacturing use, nearly tripling the planned Microsoft campus to support up to 17 total data center buildings.
Microsoft held a groundbreaking ceremony for the $1 billion La Porte campus expansion; Mayor Tom Dermody called it a defining moment for the community.
NIPSCO confirmed it is working directly with Microsoft to supply power for the expanded La Porte campus, including a new substation as part of the first construction phase.
